1.1.html:
In one line

A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing elements that appears to its users as a single coherent system. The other standard wording says the same thing from the network's side: a system in which hardware or software components located at networked computers communicate and coordinate their actions only by passing messages.

The explanation

Each half of the first definition does a separate job, and dropping either half loses marks. Autonomous computing elements means every node keeps its own clock and its own idea of what time it is, makes its own decisions, and can fail on its own. Nothing is in charge of the whole system, and that is what makes distribution hard rather than merely spread out. Single coherent system is the other half: the user should not have to know which machine holds their file, how many machines are involved, or that any of them are remote. Hiding all three is the transparency goal, and it is what separates a distributed system from a set of computers that merely happen to be networked.

Two consequences follow from autonomy combined with message passing alone. Because each node has its own clock, there is no global time to order events with. Because nodes only pass messages, everything one node knows about another arrived as a message and can therefore be late or lost.

The definition forces three characteristics, and each one is the reason a later topic exists: concurrency, no global clock and independent failures.

  • Concurrency — programs running on different machines share resources and execute at the same time, which is what lets work run on many machines at once and raises throughput. It also means two nodes may want the same resource at the same moment, and that contention is what mutual exclusion solves.
  • No global clock — each machine keeps its own time and there is no single universal time, so synchronisation across a network is difficult. Clock synchronisation brings the clocks close, and logical clocks order events when they cannot be made exact.
  • Independent failures — any single component can fail without bringing the system down, so the system has to tolerate partial failure: some part is broken and the rest keeps working. Replication, and consistency between the copies, follow from it.

Beyond those three, a distributed system is expected to have six further properties: heterogeneity (components differ in network, hardware architecture, operating system, language and implementation, and still work together), openness (services offered through published, standard interfaces, such as REST APIs), security (confidentiality, integrity and availability held over networks nobody controls), scalability (it keeps working as it grows in size, geography and administration), transparency (separate machines look like one) and fault tolerance (failures are masked and the system recovers).

The advantages and the disadvantages are the same properties seen from opposite sides. Economics — a collection of microprocessors gives better price and performance than one large machine — is the commercial argument for distributing a system; scalability, data and resource sharing, flexibility and communication are the rest. Security is the price, because every connection and every node has to be secured; loss of data while it moves across nodes, the far greater complexity of the software, and distribution of control — administration and fault-finding across machines no single node can see whole — are the others.

How it runs

A single file write shows why the definition is shaped the way it is. A client on one machine asks a file service on a second machine to write a block; the file service forwards the block to a third machine that holds the replica, and each of the three stamps the operation with its own clock.

The client's timestamp can read earlier than the timestamp on the write it caused, because the two clocks have drifted apart and nothing corrects them. Order between the operations therefore has to come from the messages themselves, not from the clocks — which is exactly the no-global-clock characteristic in action.

If the replica does not answer, the file service can still reply to the client: the write is durable where it was applied, one copy is behind, and the file remains readable. That is partial failure, and the client never learns that a third machine was involved or that one of them is behind. Autonomy, message passing and coherence are all visible in one operation.

Exam traps

  • A network of computers is not a distributed system by itself. Without the single-coherent-system half, there is no distribution in the sense the definition means — there is a set of machines that can talk to each other.
  • The three characteristics are consequences of the definition, not benefits. Writing them as advantages mixes two lists that are asked for separately.
  • Autonomy is about clocks, decisions and failure, not about hardware being unrelated or owned by different people.
  • The phrase for a single component's failure is partial failure. "The system fails" throws away the property the definition is built on.
  • Transparency, heterogeneity, openness, security, scalability and fault tolerance are further properties. Presenting them as the characteristics the definition forces is the commonest slip on this question.
  • Attribute the two definitions — Tanenbaum and Van Steen, and Coulouris — and say which one is being unpacked before unpacking it.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the definition in full, both halves, with the attribution.
  2. Unpack autonomy: own clock, own decisions, own failure, nothing in charge.
  3. Unpack the single coherent system: access, location and failure differences are hidden from the user.
  4. State that coordination happens only by passing messages, and draw the two consequences — no global time, and knowledge of a remote node is only ever a message.
  5. List the three characteristics the definition forces, one line each with the topic it leads to.
  6. List the further properties in a second, clearly separate group.
  7. Pair the advantages against the disadvantages, property by property.
  8. Close with one worked example — GFS, HDFS or BitTorrent — and name the property it demonstrates.
points: Each node keeps its own clock, decides for itself and can fail on its own, so nothing is in charge of the whole.
The user need not know which machine holds a file, how many machines are involved, or that any of them are remote.
Hardware or software components communicate and coordinate their actions only by passing messages — there is no shared memory and no shared clock.
Programs on different machines share resources and run at the same time, and two nodes may want the same resource at the same moment.
Each machine keeps its own time, so events are ordered by message passing, by clock synchronisation, or by logical clocks.
Any component may fail without bringing the system down, so partial failure has to be tolerated.
Heterogeneity, openness, security, scalability, transparency and fault tolerance.
The same properties from opposite sides: sharing, economics and scalability against security exposure, complexity and distributed control.

1.2.html:
In one line

The four goals of a distributed system are resource sharing, openness, transparency and scalability: what the system shares, how others build on it, what it hides, and how it grows.

The explanation

Resource sharing is the goal the whole exercise exists for: remote data, files, printers, processors and storage used efficiently, so that pooled resources beat buying every node its own. Users share three kinds of thing — hardware such as a printer, data such as files, and specific functionality such as a search engine — and each shared resource widens the surface that security has to cover.

Openness means services are specified through standard rules, and their syntax and semantics are written down in an interface defined in an IDL. The interface names the function, its parameters, its return values, the exceptions it can raise and how the service is used, and it is neutral: it commits to no language and no platform. Openness buys interoperability, where two implementations can use each other's services, and portability, where an application written for one distributed system runs correctly on another that implements the same interfaces. The first practical step is publishing the documentation of the components and their interfaces so that others can build against them.

Transparency is not one property but a family of eight forms, and this list is the one examiners ask for by name: access (differences in data representation and in how a resource is reached), location (where the resource physically is), migration (that a resource may move, with its name unchanged), relocation (that it may move while in use), replication (that extra copies exist), concurrency (that others are sharing the resource), failure (that a component failed and was recovered from) and persistence (whether the resource is in memory or on disk).

Scalability is the goal that keeps the other three working as the system grows, and it has four things to hold under control: the cost of physical resources, which should rise linearly with size rather than faster; the loss of performance, so a system twice the size is not dramatically slower per operation; software resources such as address space, file descriptors, port numbers and names, which must not run out; and performance bottlenecks, which are answered with decentralised algorithms that have no single node everyone must talk to, plus caching and replication.

The four goals exist because four problems stand between the system and them: heterogeneity, reliability, security and scalability. Heterogeneity is masked by middleware — a layer supplying a programming abstraction over networks, hardware, operating systems and languages, as CORBA, ODBC, JDBC and RMI do — by internet protocols, which every node already speaks, and by mobile code, which travels to the data instead of the data travelling to the code. The three differ in reach: middleware hides differences inside one organisation and hands the application an abstraction it can call, internet protocols hide them across the whole world at the price of the lowest common denominator, and mobile code removes the assumption that a program stays where it was written. Reliability separates availability, the fraction of time a system is usable, from running continuously without interruption — a machine down for a millisecond every hour is highly available and still unreliable, and one that never crashes but shuts for two fixed weeks each year is highly reliable and only about 96% available. Redundancy is what raises availability. Security holds the CIA triad — confidentiality, integrity and availability — through encryption, authentication and authorisation, and stays hard because of denial-of-service attacks, which attack availability directly, and the security of mobile code. Scalability splits into size, geographical and administrative, and administrative is the hardest because its obstacles are organisational and human rather than technical.

How it runs

Watch the four goals meet in one shared file service. A file is published through an interface naming read, write and delete rather than being handed out as a file: that interface is the openness goal, because any platform implementing it can use the service.

The client calls it by the same path it would use locally, so the location of the file and the three copies of it are invisible — access, location and replication transparency in one operation. A second client reading the same file at the same time must be serialised against the first, which is concurrency transparency.

When traffic grows, replicas are added and the name does not change, and the cost of storage rises with the number of copies rather than faster than it — the scalability goal, held by a decentralised placement of work plus caching and replication. Shared resource, published interface, hidden copies, controlled growth: all four goals in one service.

Exam traps

  • Transparency is a family, not a single property. A one-line "transparency hides the details" answer cannot earn the marks the list carries.
  • Availability and reliability are not synonyms, and the pair of examples — a millisecond an hour against two weeks a year — is usually what the question is checking.
  • Middleware, internet protocols and mobile code are three distinct answers to heterogeneity. They are not three names for the same mechanism.
  • The four goals are resource sharing, openness, transparency and scalability. The four problems are heterogeneity, reliability, security and scalability; mixing the two lists is a common error.
  • Administrative scalability is the hardest of the three kinds, and the answer needs the reason — the obstacles are organisational and human.
  • An IDL is neutral about language and platform. Saying it "defines the service" without saying it describes parameters, return values and exceptions leaves marks on the table.

Full-marks answer

  1. Name the four goals in one line, in order.
  2. Resource sharing: the three kinds of shared thing, the efficiency argument, and the security cost.
  3. Openness: standard rules, the interface in an IDL, what the interface describes, then interoperability and portability.
  4. Transparency: the eight forms as a named list, one clause each.
  5. Scalability: the four things to control, then decentralised algorithms, caching and replication.
  6. Turn to the four problems and give the treatment for each: middleware, internet protocols and mobile code for heterogeneity; availability, redundancy and fault tolerance for reliability; the CIA triad and its mechanisms for security; the three kinds of scalability for scalability.
  7. Close on why the goals matter together: each answers a different question, and a system that meets some but not all is distributed without being usable.
points: Remote data, files, printers, processors and storage used efficiently — the motivation for building a distributed system at all.
Services specified through standard rules and an interface written in an IDL, neutral about language and platform.
Two implementations use each other's services; an application written for one system runs correctly on another.
Eight forms: access, location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure and persistence.
Four things held under control: the cost of physical resources, lost performance, software resources running out, and bottlenecks.
Masked by middleware, by internet protocols and by mobile code — three answers with different reach.
Availability is the fraction of time a system is usable, and redundancy is what raises it; it is not the same as running continuously.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability, kept by encryption, authentication and authorisation.
A resource is the thing itself; a service is the interface that manages a collection of related resources and decides who may use them.

1.3.t: Examples: Google File System, Hadoop, BitTorrent, etc
1.3.html:
In one line

GFS, HDFS and BitTorrent are the three worked examples of distributed systems here: two shared file systems built on one distinguished metadata node, and one peer-to-peer network with no distinguished node at all.

The explanation

The Google File System is Google's cluster file system. A single master holds the metadata, files are split into large chunks, and each chunk is replicated across many chunk servers. It is built precisely because components fail: failure is treated as normal rather than exceptional, and the design earns its keep by continuing to serve files while individual chunk servers are unavailable. Everything a reader needs to explain distributed systems is in that shape — autonomous nodes, a network between them, one file system presented to the user, and replication standing in for reliability.

HDFS is the open-source descendant of GFS, paired with MapReduce. It runs a NameNode for metadata and many DataNodes holding replicated blocks. The same shape, for the same reason, on commodity machines: files look like one system while storage and computation are spread across hardware that is expected to break.

BitTorrent is the opposite arrangement and the clearest illustration of the peer-to-peer model. A file is split into pieces, and every peer that holds pieces also serves them, so there is no client and no server and any one computer holds only a small part of the data. Capacity grows with the number of participants rather than with the size of one machine, and no single node's failure ends the service.

These three are the examples, and the applications that motivate the field are worth naming as a group: web search, finance and commerce, the creative industries and entertainment, healthcare, education, transport and logistics, massive online multiplayer games, and financial trading. The last two are the demanding ones, because both need low and predictable latency across the world — which is what pushes computation back out towards the user, the thread that runs on into edge and fog computing.

The Web is the largest distributed system in existence and its own difficulties are distribution problems seen in the wild: dangling links, where a resource is deleted and the links to it remain; slow response to users; and the lack of a proper user interface. Each is a symptom of the same cause — the parts are independent and nobody is in charge of the whole — which is why they cannot be fixed by making the machines faster. The Web also solves the scalability goal rather than failing it: caching and replication in many places, with no single node everybody must talk to, is what lets it serve the world.

How it runs

A write to a system shaped like GFS, step by step. The client asks the master where the first chunk of the file should go, and the master replies with the holding chunk servers rather than with the data itself, so that the metadata node never becomes the path every byte travels.

The client sends the chunk to one chunk server and that server forwards it to the other replicas, so the client's own link carries the chunk once instead of once per copy. Each replica writes to its local disk and acknowledges; when the acknowledgements arrive, the client reports the write as complete.

Meanwhile the master's reply was a lease, not a permanent assignment, so the same design survives the failure of the chunk server the client happens to be talking to: the lease expires, the master names a different replica, and the file is still readable throughout. One distinguished node for metadata, many autonomous nodes for bytes, and failure treated as an ordinary event rather than an emergency.

Exam traps

  • GFS and HDFS are the same architecture, not two unrelated systems. The answer should say HDFS is the open-source descendant and MapReduce is its companion, not a replacement for the file system.
  • Name the parts with the terms the design uses — master and chunk servers for GFS, NameNode and DataNodes for HDFS — instead of "a server and some storage".
  • BitTorrent illustrates the peer-to-peer model; using it as an example of client-server loses the point of the example.
  • The metadata node is a single point of failure in both file systems, and that fact is a mark-earning observation about the model rather than a defect to be hidden.
  • The Web's difficulties — dangling links, slow responses, no proper user interface — are asked for as a list, and each needs the reason it arises from distribution.
  • The applications list is not filler: naming the latency-critical ones (multiplayer games, financial trading) and why they are the hard cases shows the field is understood rather than recited.

Full-marks answer

  1. Introduce the three examples in one sentence, grouped by model: two shared file systems and one peer-to-peer network.
  2. GFS: master, large chunks, replicated chunk servers, failure treated as normal.
  3. HDFS: the descendant of GFS plus MapReduce, with a NameNode and DataNodes holding replicated blocks.
  4. BitTorrent: pieces, peers serving what they hold, no central server, capacity growing with the participants.
  5. Contrast the models in a line: a distinguished node gives simplicity and authority at the cost of a bottleneck; symmetry removes the bottleneck and adds placement, discovery and replica maintenance.
  6. List the application areas, and mark the ones where latency across the world is the binding constraint.
  7. Treat the Web as the live case: its three difficulties with the cause of each, and the caching and replication that let it scale.
points: A single master holds the metadata, files are split into large chunks, and chunks are replicated across many chunk servers.
The open-source descendant of GFS plus MapReduce: a NameNode for metadata and many DataNodes holding replicated blocks.
A file is split into pieces and every peer that holds pieces also serves them — no client and no server, and no central point of failure.
Both file systems are built for machines that fail, so failure is treated as normal rather than exceptional.
Three difficulties of distribution seen in the wild: dangling links, slow response to users, and the lack of a proper user interface.
Web search, finance and commerce, entertainment, healthcare, education, transport, multiplayer games and financial trading.

1.4.html:
In one line

Three architecture models describe where the parts sit and how they relate — client-server, peer-to-peer and multitier — while fundamental models describe the properties every architecture shares, and distributed systems themselves come in three types: cluster, grid and cloud.

The explanation

Client-server is the base pattern, built on request and reply: the client sends a request asking for a service, and the server does the work and returns either the result or an error code. In practice the exchange runs over send and receive primitives, or through RPC or RMI so that a remote call reads like a local one. The strength is authority: one distinguished process owns the service, so one place controls access and one place knows the state. The weakness comes from the same concentration — that server is a bottleneck and a single point of failure, and peers cannot be added to scale it. The pair to hold in mind is a web browser and a web server, or an NFS client and a file server.

Peer-to-peer removes the distinction entirely: all processes play the same role, the pattern of communication depends on the application, and a large number of data objects are shared with any one computer holding only a small part of the application database. Processing and communication load spread across many computers and links, which makes it the most general and most flexible model. Three problems follow from the symmetry: objects must be placed cleverly, the needed objects must be found among many peers, and a potentially large number of replicas must be kept equal. In exchange, availability needs no distinguished server — no single node's failure ends the service, and capacity grows with the number of participants. BitTorrent is the example.

Multitier extends client-server into layers so that each tier can be scaled and replaced on its own. The three-tier application is the clearest case: a presentation tier holding what the user sees, an application tier (also called the logic tier) holding the decisions, and a data tier holding the state. Split by function, the same system serves thousands of clients from a handful of logic servers. The logic tier is where servers are added as load grows; the data tier is the one that cannot simply be copied without asking how the copies are kept equal, which is why consistency becomes a topic in its own right. A three-tier application is a distributed system because the tiers are the distribution and they talk over the network exactly as any client and server do.

Fundamental models describe, more formally, the properties common to all of the above. The interaction model describes how processes communicate and coordinate — the flow of information plus the synchronisation and ordering of activities between processes — and it reflects the fact that communication takes place with delays. The failure model defines and classifies faults so that behaviour stays predictable when things break, with the classes omission, timing and arbitrary failures, and a system built on it works as predicted only as long as the real faults behave as the model says. The security model defines and classifies forms of attack, giving a basis for analysing threats and a way to design systems that resist them.

Putting time limits on process execution, message delivery or clock drift is hard in a distributed system, and whether those limits may be assumed is exactly what separates the two variants of the interaction model. In a synchronous distributed system, each step has a known lower and upper time bound, every message is received within a known bounded time, and each clock's drift from real time has a known bound — so a time limit can be put on a reply and a timeout treated as a failure. In an asynchronous distributed system, none of the three is bounded: a step may take arbitrarily long, a message may be received after an arbitrarily long time, and the drift rate is arbitrary — so no such limit can be assumed, and a slow node looks exactly like a dead one.

Finally, the three types. A cluster is a parallel or distributed processing system of interconnected stand-alone computers working cooperatively as one integrated computing resource; its defining feature is homogeneity — the computers run the same operating system and sit on the same network — and it is used for highly scalable services such as search engines and for parallel programming. A grid enables the sharing, selection and aggregation of geographically distributed autonomous resources dynamically at runtime, depending on availability, capability, performance, cost and quality of service; its defining feature is a high degree of heterogeneity, and it is built in five layers. A cloud provides shared processing resources and data on demand, metered and elastic, from a shared pool of configurable resources, in the service models SaaS, PaaS and IaaS.

The grid's five layers are a hierarchy of dependence, each using the one below: fabric, which interfaces to the local resources at a site so they can be shared inside a virtual organisation; connectivity, the communication protocols supporting grid transactions, including the delegation of rights from authenticated users to programs running on their behalf; resource, which manages a single resource and enforces access control; collective, which handles access to multiple resources — discovery, allocation, scheduling and data replication; and application, the applications using the services. Only the fabric layer touches resources physically installed somewhere. What holds the layers together is the virtual organisation: a set of users and institutions sharing resources under agreed rules, with the connectivity layer delegating exactly the rights a user holds and no more.

How it runs

A three-tier application under load, followed through the tiers. Thousands of clients hold only a presentation layer; each sends a request over the network to one of a handful of application servers, which is where the decisions are taken. Those servers read and write through the data tier, which holds the state.

When traffic doubles, application servers are added behind the same address, and the presentation tier is untouched — that is the point of splitting by function. The data tier cannot be scaled the same way: a copy of it is not the same data unless the copies are kept equal, so replication there brings the consistency question with it.

Now break the middle tier. The request arrives at the wrong application server, which answers from its own cache for a moment and is then withdrawn from the pool by the load balancer. Nothing about the failure reaches the presentation tier, and the answer is late rather than absent — which is a failure model question, not an availability question, and shows why the two layers of description are kept apart.

Exam traps

  • Architecture models describe placement and relationships; fundamental models describe properties common to all architectures. Confusing the two is the standing trap on this question.
  • Client-server is one property, not a picture: a distinguished process owns the service. Both its strength (authority) and its weakness (bottleneck, single point of failure) follow from that one property and should be written that way.
  • The three peer-to-peer problems are placement, retrieval and replica maintenance. A general remark about "complexity" does not earn those marks.
  • Synchronous and asynchronous differ in exactly three assumptions — process execution, message delivery and clock drift — and the payoff is the last line: a timeout can be treated as a failure only in the synchronous model.
  • Cluster and grid are told apart by homogeneity and geography. The cloud adds on-demand metered access to a shared pool on top of grid-like infrastructure, so it is not simply "the grid, but newer".
  • The grid's five layers are a named, ordered list: fabric, connectivity, resource, collective, application. The virtual organisation is the idea that holds them together, and rights delegation is the connectivity layer's job.

Full-marks answer

  1. State the split: architecture models for placement, fundamental models for shared properties.
  2. Client-server: the request and reply, the primitives and the RPC and RMI variants, authority as the strength, bottleneck and single point of failure as the cost, with an example pair.
  3. Peer-to-peer: all processes equal, data objects spread, load spread, the three problems, and availability without a distinguished node.
  4. Multitier: presentation, application and data tiers; each scaled and replaced on its own; the data tier's replication question leading to consistency.
  5. Fundamental models: interaction, failure and security, one line each, naming the failure classes.
  6. Synchronous against asynchronous, in a small table of the three assumptions, ending with the timeout consequence.
  7. Cluster, grid and cloud, told apart by homogeneity, geography and on-demand metered access.
  8. Finish with the grid's five layers in order, and the virtual organisation as the reason they hold together.
points: Client-server, peer-to-peer and multitier describe the placement of the parts and the relationships between them.
A request-reply pair with a distinguished server: one place holds the state, enforces access and fails — which is both the strength and the cost.
Every process plays the same role; three problems follow — placing objects, retrieving them among many peers, and keeping replicas equal.
Presentation, application and data tiers, each scaled and replaced on its own; the data tier raises the consistency question.
Interaction, failure and security — the properties common to every architecture.
Process execution, message delivery and clock drift are all bounded, so a timeout can be treated as a failure.
None of the three is bounded, so a slow node and a dead node look identical.
Homogeneous and local; heterogeneous and geographically distributed; on-demand metered access to a shared pool.
The five layers of a grid
Fabric, connectivity, resource, collective and application, held together by the virtual organisation.

2.0.html:
In one line

Following the object-oriented programming model, objects distributed across different address spaces that work together by sharing data and invoking methods are termed distributed objects; those address spaces may be several processes on one computer, or processes on different computers in a network.

The explanation

Three properties of that definition carry the weight. The objects are the communicating entities: processes do not exchange raw bytes by hand, they invoke methods on each other. The abstraction is what hides the complexity of distributed programming from the programmer. And location transparency is what the abstraction buys — because a caller does not know where the object is, distributed objects generally communicate using RMI.

A local object and a distributed object are not equivalent, and the model says so. Six areas separate them, and each one is the reason some later mechanism exists:

  • Reference — a local reference is a pointer into the same address space, one machine word. Remotely, a reference has to be meaningful in another address space, which is why the remote object reference and the binder exist.
  • Request latency — a local call takes a few instructions and is bounded by memory speed; every remote call crosses a network, so latency is orders of magnitude larger and variable, and a design that makes many small calls performs badly.
  • Object activation — a local object is in memory because its process is running; a remote object may not be instantiated yet, so a call may have to activate it first.
  • Parallelism — two calls on a local object are serialised by its process; remote calls can arrive from several clients at once, so the object's behaviour in a concurrent environment becomes the implementer's problem.
  • Failure — locally the process either works or it does not; remotely a call can be lost, the server can crash after executing, or the client can crash after asking. This is partial failure, and it produces the whole of call semantics.
  • Security — locally the operating system enforces access; remotely data crosses a network between parties that need not trust each other, so access control and authentication move into the middleware.

Two mechanisms are used for communication between distributed objects: RPC and RMI. Under both of them sits the message layer.

How it runs

A single method call on a remote object, watched from the caller's side. The caller holds something that looks like a reference to the object, calls a method on it, and waits — exactly as with a local object, because that is the point of the abstraction.

Underneath, the reference is not an address: it is a remote object reference that has to be resolved, which costs a lookup, and the call itself has to be turned into a message and sent. The time it takes is not a few instructions but a network round trip, and its length depends on the network rather than on the object.

The object on the far side may not be running yet, so the call may trigger its activation before the method body executes. If the reply never comes, the caller has a case no local call can produce: the method may have run, may not have run, or may have run and been lost — and nothing in the caller's code decides which. That single uncertainty is why invocation semantics are a design decision rather than a detail.

Exam traps

  • Do not say the distributed object model makes a local object and a remote object the same. The model says explicitly that they are not equivalent, and the six areas are the marks.
  • Reproduce the six areas as a named list — reference, request latency, object activation, parallelism, failure, security. Each needs its consequence, not just its name.
  • Failure in this list means partial failure, and the answer should say that it produces call semantics; leaving it at "the network can fail" skips the point.
  • Security leaving the operating system is the part most often forgotten. Access control and authentication move into the middleware.
  • Location transparency is what the abstraction buys, and it is why distributed objects use RMI rather than message passing at the application level.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define distributed objects in the object-oriented terms, and note that the address spaces may share a machine or be on different machines.
  2. Give the three properties: objects are the communicating entities; the abstraction hides complexity; location transparency is what it buys.
  3. State that a local object and a distributed object are not equivalent.
  4. Work through the six areas, one line of local reality and one of consequence each.
  5. Name partial failure as the source of call semantics.
  6. Close by naming the two mechanisms for communication between distributed objects — RPC and RMI — and which follows from which.

2.1.html:
In one line

An RPC is an interaction between a client and a server in which the client invokes a procedure that resides remotely on the server; the server executes the procedure and passes the result back, and the client's call is blocked from the moment it calls until the result arrives.

The explanation

RPC is built on the single-process procedure-call model — that is the entire point of its name — and it is therefore a high-level network communication interface rather than a low-level one. The caller pays with blocking, and receives the ordinary procedure-call model in exchange. A server process exposes a service interface defining the procedures available for remote calling, and works under a request–reply protocol that deliberately leaves the object reference out of request messages: the request names a procedure, not an object.

Simple RPC does not maintain access transparency: the data representation and the method of object access are not hidden from the programmer, so a remote call does not look exactly like a local one. Keeping access transparency is what the stub layer exists to fix, and what the proxy layer formalises in RMI.

The mechanism is a sequence of ten steps — steps 1 to 3 on the client side, 4 to 7 on the server side, and 8 to 10 for the reply. The client procedure calls the client stub as an ordinary local call. The client stub builds a message containing the parameters and the name or number of the procedure, and calls the local operating system; packaging the arguments into a network message is marshalling. The client sends the message to the remote operating system through a system call, over a connectionless or connection-oriented protocol. The remote operating system hands the message to the server stub, which unpacks the parameters — unmarshalling — and calls the server. The server does the work; the server stub packs the result, the server's operating system sends it, the client's operating system delivers it, and the client stub unpacks the result and returns it to the waiting procedure. The middle of the sequence is where the abstraction lives: the client procedure never learns it spoke to a stub, and the server procedure never learns it was called across a network.

The benefits and the costs are the same fact seen twice. The called procedure runs in a different process on a different machine; process and thread models are supported; a complete stub layer gives access transparency; and code is reusable, with the same call working locally and in a distributed environment. The costs: only call-by-value and call-by-reference parameters are supported, which is not always acceptable; overheads of marshalling, the network round trip and kernel calls at both ends make it slower; and the marshalled representation must be agreed at both ends, so it is inflexible about hardware architectures. Two of those costs each start a later topic. Call-by-reference sends a pointer into another address space, where it means nothing, and the repair is the remote object reference and the stub. Representation inflexibility is why the interface has to be expressed in something language-neutral — an IDL, or a data format such as JSON.

Because the caller and the provider sit in distant places, normal functioning can be disrupted in five ways, and each has a mechanism that answers it. The client may be unable to locate the server, which is a binding failure answered by a naming or binder service. A request may be lost, which the client cannot distinguish from a slow server, and the answer is to retransmit after a timeout. A reply may be lost, so the operation was in fact performed and the client never learns the result; the answers are retransmission or a history of results. The server may crash after receiving a request, leaving the client unable to know whether the procedure ran, which duplicate filtering and idempotent operation design address. The client may crash after sending a request, leaving an orphan call whose result nobody will collect, and orphans are detected and discarded.

Under those faults, call semantics define when and how often a remote procedure may be executed, and they must be the same whether the procedure is implemented locally or remotely — otherwise the abstraction leaks and the program becomes untestable. Exactly once is the ideal: time-outs, retransmissions, the same call identifier on every retransmission, and a cache at the callee that recognises a repeat. At most once, also called maybe, guarantees execution once or not at all, with the client unable to tell which, because the RPC is requested once and never retried. At least once guarantees one or more executions if a reply arrives at all, since the client keeps requesting until a valid response does, and it is safe only when repeating the operation is harmless. Last once counts only the most recent call's result, using time-outs and retransmission. Last-of-many accepts a call only when the identifier matches the most recent one, neglecting orphan calls. Every step down that list buys reliability of delivery at the cost of knowing less about how many times the work happened, and the engineering repair for repeats is an idempotent operation.

Underneath the semantics sit three fault-tolerant measures, and each is a decision with a price. Retrying the request message risks the at-least-once hazard. Duplicate filtering, used when retransmissions happen, makes the server remember identifiers of requests it has seen, which costs state and time. Retransmission of results keeps a history of result messages so that a lost reply can be answered without re-executing the operation. The third is the fix for the most awkward fault, because a lost reply means the work was already done and re-executing it is exactly the wrong response.

How it runs

Follow one call through all ten steps, with the failure cases attached to the step that can produce them. Steps 1 to 3 are local work: the procedure calls its stub, the stub marshals parameters and the procedure number into a message, and the local kernel sends it.

Between step 3 and step 6 there is nothing but the network, and this is where the first two faults live: if the server cannot be located there is no route at all, and if the request is lost the client sees only silence. The client is blocked throughout, so it cannot tell a lost request from a slow server — the reason a request is retransmitted only after a timeout, and the reason that retransmission raises the at-least-once hazard.

Steps 4 to 7 are the server's side, and the crash fault sits here: the server stub unmarshals and calls the server, and the server may die after the work is done but before the result is packed, leaving the client with no way to know whether the procedure ran. Steps 8 to 10 carry the reply, where the lost-reply fault lives: the work is done, the result is gone, and the correct answer is a stored result rather than a second execution.

Exam traps

  • The ten steps are asked for as a sequence, with the side each step belongs to. An answer that describes "the client sends a message and the server replies" is not the sequence.
  • Marshalling happens on the way out and unmarshalling on the way in, and both happen twice in one call — once for the arguments and once for the result.
  • The five faults each need their own mechanism. Giving retransmission for all five loses the marks for locating the server, duplicate filtering and orphan detection.
  • Exactly once is the ideal and is hard to achieve; at most once can execute zero times and at least once can execute twice. The trade-off in that sentence is the answer, not the table alone.
  • Idempotent is the word that repairs repeats. Repeating an operation that is not idempotent is the hazard, not the solution.
  • The request message names a procedure, not an object. That deliberate omission is what separates RPC from RMI.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define RPC, including that the caller blocks until the result arrives, and place it as a high-level interface built on the single-process call model.
  2. Describe the service interface and the request–reply protocol, and state that the request names a procedure rather than an object.
  3. Note that access transparency needs the stub layer.
  4. Give the ten steps in order, marking the client side, the server side and the reply, and naming marshalling and unmarshalling where they occur.
  5. List the benefits and the costs in pairs, and give the reason each cost arises.
  6. Give the five faults with the mechanism that answers each, then state why call semantics have to be defined.
  7. Give the five semantics from exactly once down to last-of-many, with the guarantee of each and the price of it, and name idempotency as the repair.
  8. Finish with the three fault-tolerant measures — retry, duplicate filtering, retransmission of results — and say which fault the third one exists for.

Steps 1 to 3 are the client side, 4 to 7 the server side and 8 to 10 the reply, and the client procedure is blocked throughout.
The client stub packs the parameters and the procedure number into a message; unmarshalling is the server stub unpacking them.
Another process or machine, and code reusability, bought with call-by-value and call-by-reference only, overheads, and a representation both ends must agree.
The server cannot be located, the request is lost, the reply is lost, the server crashes after the request, or the client crashes after sending.
Exactly once, at most once or maybe, at least once, last once, and last-of-many.
An operation repeatable with the same effect — the repair for a retransmission that would otherwise execute the procedure twice.
Three measures: retry the request message, filter duplicate requests, and retransmit stored results.

2.2.html:
In one line

RMI is a communication mechanism among distributed objects in which method invocation between objects in different processes takes place, whether those processes are on the same machine or separated — and where RPC invokes a procedure by name and drops the object reference, RMI keeps the object.

The explanation

Each process consists of a set of objects, and those objects may receive local invocations, remote invocations, or both. Objects that receive remote invocations are remote objects. The caller holds a reference to an object that happens to live in another process and calls a method on it, which is what forces the extra machinery RPC does not need.

A remote invocation meets three requirements, in this order. The caller must hold a remote object reference for the object — the repaired version of the pointer RPC cannot send. The object must have a remote interface specifying which of its methods can be invoked remotely, and only those can be invoked from outside; everything else is private to the process that holds the object. And the object itself is a remote object, whose class usually also has to be usable by a local caller, so the implementation is separated from what is exposed. Nothing visible from outside distinguishes an object that can receive remote invocations from one that cannot — only the interface does.

The software that implements this has five roles to name. A proxy makes remote invocation transparent to the client: it marshals arguments, forwards the request, receives the message and unmarshals results, behaving from the client's side like the object itself. A dispatcher receives requests, selects the correct method and passes the request message on. A skeleton implements the methods of the remote interface: it unmarshals arguments, invokes the method of the remote object and marshals the results. The remote reference module translates between local and remote object references and keeps the remote object table, holding an entry for each remote object and each local proxy, creating a remote object reference when one arrives and looking entries up when one must be passed. A binder is a separate service keeping a table of mappings from textual names to remote object references: servers register objects with it and clients look references up in it. Two further pieces of the server side matter: server threads, since a call is handled by creating a new thread for each remote invocation, and the division of labour between the programs — the server holds the dispatchers, skeletons and remote objects plus the code registering them with the binder, and the client holds the proxies and the binder lookup. One practical consequence: a client cannot create remote objects by calling constructors directly, so remote object creation goes through factory methods.

The remote interface is the boundary of what can be invoked from outside, and its two implementations are the comparison to hold. CORBA specifies it in an IDL, which is language-neutral: the interface is written once and implementations may be in C++, Java or anything else. Java RMI extends the interface with the Remote keyword — public interface HelloInterface extends Remote — which is convenient, and in exchange both ends must be Java. The invocation semantics are the second half of the same trade: CORBA uses at-most-once, and maybe semantics for methods that do not return a result, while Java RMI uses at-most-once.

RMI shares RPC's design issues in three respects — programming with interfaces, call semantics, and the level of transparency — and adds two of its own: the number of times the method is invoked in response to a single remote invocation, and how much location transparency is provided. The invocation semantics are the same family as RPC's with the same failure analysis attached. Exactly once executes every method exactly once, which is the ideal. Maybe leaves the invoker unable to determine whether the remote method ran, with omission failures when the invocation or the result message is lost and crash failures when the server holding the object fails; it is useful where an occasional failed invocation is acceptable. At-least-once gives the invoker either a result, so the method ran at least once, or an exception; retransmitting the request masks omission failures, crash failures remain, and the hazard is arbitrary failure because the method may run more than once — repaired by designing operations as idempotent. At-most-once gives a result, with the method executed at most once, or an exception, using every fault-tolerance method: omission failures are eliminated by retransmitting and arbitrary failures prevented by ensuring nothing runs twice. Java RMI and CORBA use at-most-once; CORBA also uses maybe for methods that return nothing; SUNRPC provides at-least-once.

Location transparency is where the model collides with reality. Attempting full location transparency causes both failure and latency, because a remote invocation differs syntactically from a local one. Two solutions are named: exceptions and exception handling, so that the language's error mechanism carries the ways a remote call can fail; or deliberately weaker invocation semantics, accepting that a remote call is not a local call instead of pretending the difference does not exist. Access transparency is that the same operation is used on a remote object as on a local one, and RPC does deliver that. Location transparency is the stronger claim that the caller does not know where the object is, and that claim fails in practice, because a network's latency and its failure modes are part of the interface whether the designer admits it or not. A call dressed up as a local one leaves the programmer no way to handle what actually happens.

The Java RMI case study puts the roles into four files. The remote interface file defines what the service offers — a short statement extending Remote with a method that throws RemoteException. The remote object file implements the service with a constructor and the required functions, extending UnicastRemoteObject and implementing the interface. The client file looks the object up by name with Naming.lookup and then calls the method like a local object. The server file offers the service, installs a security manager, and contacts the rmiregistry to bind an instance of the service under the name of the remote object. Java RMI lets objects invoke methods on remote objects using the same syntax as local invocations, and type checking applies equally to both; its costs are that it is a single-language system and that the implementer of a remote object must consider its behaviour in a concurrent environment.

How it runs

One remote method call, followed through the roles. The client calls a method on what it holds — a proxy that behaves like the object. The proxy marshals the arguments and asks its communication module to send the request, and the communication module on the server side hands the message to the dispatcher.

The dispatcher reads the method identifier and selects the right method, passing the message to the skeleton. The skeleton unmarshals the arguments, invokes the method on the servant — the object itself — and marshals the result back through the same path, where the client's proxy unmarshals it and returns it to the caller as an ordinary value.

References are resolved before any of this: the client's binder lookup turns a textual name into a remote object reference, and the remote reference modules translate between local and remote references as objects are passed. A reference that travels out of the process is created on the way and looked up on the way in, which is why an object passed as a parameter is not the pointer the caller held. Two failures belong to this path and not to RPC's ten steps: the call may arrive at an object that is not instantiated yet, and several calls may arrive at once, so the method body must be written for a concurrent environment.

Exam traps

  • The five roles are a named list — proxy, dispatcher, skeleton, remote reference module, binder — and each needs its responsibility. "A stub" and "a registry" do not cover them.
  • The difference from RPC is the sentence the question is usually testing: RPC names a procedure and drops the object reference, RMI keeps the object and therefore needs references to be resolved.
  • The remote interface is a boundary the runtime enforces, not documentation. Only the methods on it can be invoked remotely.
  • Access transparency and location transparency are not the same claim, and only the second one fails in practice. Conflating them is the commonest error on this question.
  • Which system uses which semantics is asked by name: Java RMI and CORBA at-most-once, CORBA additionally maybe for methods with no result, SUNRPC at-least-once.
  • The two costs of Java RMI are single language and concurrency, and they are the two things an answer usually omits while listing its syntax.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define RMI and state the difference from RPC in one line.
  2. Give the three requirements in the order a remote invocation meets them.
  3. Describe the five software roles, one responsibility each, then server threads and the client–server split.
  4. Compare the two remote interfaces: CORBA's IDL for language neutrality against Java's Remote keyword, with the semantics each uses.
  5. List RMI's design issues, marking the three it shares with RPC and the two of its own.
  6. Give the invocation semantics with their guarantees and failure types, and name which system uses which.
  7. Explain why full location transparency fails, and give the two solutions.
  8. Close with the Java RMI case study: the four files and what each contains, then the two costs of the approach.

2.3.html:
In one line

RPC and RMI hide the message; two mechanisms sit underneath them — the message-passing model, in which the programmer writes the sends and receives, and serialization, which makes it possible to put a structured value into a message at all.

The explanation

The comparison that motivates message passing is memory. In a shared memory system all processing elements see one data area, which makes parallelising easy and all data available nearby, but it is practical only up to a certain system size because everything must share one memory. In a distributed memory system each processing element has its own memory and they meet only on a network, which makes locality of data explicit and the machine cheap to build, at the price that data moves only by explicit messages, so the programmer must think about where it is.

In the model, the work unit is the process, data units are decomposed with no shared data between them, and coordination is by the send and recv primitives — the analogy being mail. Two details of the signature matter: recv may report the number of bytes received, and the tag and the process identifier may be wildcarded. A specific send paired with a wildcarded receive is the request–reply interaction again, written out by hand.

SPMD — Single Program, Multiple Data — describes how such a program is written: all processors run the same program, but not in lockstep. It is one program and not one per processor, since each copy behaves differently from its own identity, passed in as an argument. Collective calls add global reductions such as max and sum, and broadcast; a collective call is also a synchronisation, so the slowest participant sets the pace.

MPI is the real message-passing system, and every program is bracketed by MPI_Init and MPI_Finalize with all calls lying between them. MPI_Comm_size gives the number of processes, MPI_Comm_rank gives which part of the work this process owns, and MPI_Send and MPI_Recv take a buffer, a count, a datatype, a destination or source, a tag and a communicator.

What implementing message passing costs is a list in its own right. A send and a receive copy data from the user's space on one processor to the user's space on another, with the library in between packetising it. Data copying is paid twice, into buffers at both ends. Buffer availability can make a send block if no buffer is free at the receiver. Then packetisation, tag matching and a progress engine all have work to do, and the transfer needs synchronisation, because the receiver may have to answer whether the sender may send before the data moves.

A message is an envelope — tag, communicator, length, source — plus data, and three protocols trade buffer memory against waiting. Short sends the whole message when it fits in an internal buffer, at the lowest overhead. Eager sends as soon as the data is available, whether or not the receiver is ready, giving the best latency at the cost of buffering. Rendezvous sends the header first and the data only after an ok-to-send reply, needing no large buffer at the cost of a round trip. One implementation uses all three, choosing per message.

Persistence and synchronicity decide how a message is handled. Both assume applications running on hosts, one connection each to a communication server, with buffers on the hosts or in the servers. A transient message is discarded if it cannot be delivered now; a persistent one is stored until the receiver can take it. An asynchronous sender continues immediately after submitting its message; a synchronous sender is blocked until the message is stored in a local buffer at the receiving host or delivered to the receiver. Client/server computing is generally synchronous: both parties must be active, the client issues a request and blocks, and the server waits for incoming requests. The drawbacks are that the client can do no other work while waiting and that failures must be dealt with immediately because the client is waiting — and for mail and news the model is simply not appropriate. The answer is a messaging interface in which queued messages are sent among processes, the sender is not stopped waiting for an immediate reply, and fault tolerance is often handled by middleware rather than by the application.

Finally, every mechanism here has to put a structured value into a byte stream and rebuild it at the other end. Marshalling packages arguments or a result into a message suitable for transmission; unmarshalling unpacks it back into parameters or a return value. Serialization is the general problem of converting an object or data structure into a form that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, so marshalling is serialization for the specific purpose of a call. Two things make it hard. The first is representation mismatch: two machines may disagree about byte order, integer width and floating-point format, so the serialized form has to be agreed — which is why an IDL matters. The second is the reason call-by-reference is a problem: a value can be copied into a message, but a reference is a pointer into one address space, and a pointer means nothing in another. Passing an object remotely therefore means either copying it, or passing a reference that the remote reference module can resolve.

How it runs

A single send and receive pair, with the three protocols as the possible shapes of it. The sender calls send with a buffer, a count, a datatype, a destination, a tag and a communicator; the library attaches the envelope — tag, communicator, length, source — and the pair of processes puts the packet on the network with a copy into a buffer at each end.

If the message is short, the whole of it travels in the first packet and the send returns almost immediately. If the receiver is known to be ready, the eager protocol does the same for a large message, sending it as soon as it exists and accepting that a buffer has to hold it meanwhile. If it is not, the rendezvous protocol sends the header alone and waits: the receiver answers that it is ready, and only then does the data move — one round trip, and no large buffer anywhere.

The receive side matches the incoming envelope against the arguments of recv, which may wildcard the tag and the sending process, and copies the payload into the receiver's buffer. Anything not yet delivered is either thrown away or stored, depending on whether the message is transient or persistent, and whether the sender blocked on it or continued decides whether the two processes are doing work at the same time or one is waiting on the other.

Exam traps

  • Shared memory and distributed memory are compared on two axes — the advantage and the limitation of each. Presenting only the advantage loses half the marks.
  • The three protocols are short, eager and rendezvous, and each trades buffer memory against waiting. Naming them without the trade is a list, not an answer.
  • Transient against persistent is about what happens when the message cannot be delivered now; asynchronous against synchronous is about what the sender does next. They are independent questions.
  • Client/server computing is synchronous, and its two drawbacks — the client cannot work while waiting, and failures must be handled immediately — are the reason the messaging interface exists.
  • Marshalling, unmarshalling and serialization are not synonyms in this unit: marshalling is serialization for a call, and it happens once for the arguments and once for the result.
  • Representation mismatch and call-by-reference are the two reasons serialization is hard, and the second one is the same fact that appears in RPC's disadvantage list.

Full-marks answer

  1. State the two mechanisms under RPC and RMI, and define each in a line.
  2. Compare shared memory against distributed memory on advantage and limitation.
  3. Give the model: the process as work unit, decomposed data with no sharing, coordination by send and recv, the mail analogy, and the wildcarded signature fields.
  4. Describe SPMD and collective calls, noting that a collective call synchronises.
  5. List the MPI calls that bracket a program and the calls that give size, rank and transfer.
  6. Give the costs of implementation — double copying, buffer availability, packetisation, tag matching, progress engine, synchronisation.
  7. Give the message envelope and the three protocols with the trade each makes.
  8. Finish with persistence and synchronicity, the synchronous client/server model and its two drawbacks, the queued-message answer, and then serialization: marshalling, unmarshalling, representation mismatch and the call-by-reference problem.

2.4.html:
In one line

Sockets are the low-level primitive under every mechanism above — channels formed across a network with the operating system's help, each end an endpoint object bound to a local port — and web services are message passing between programs that were never written to cooperate, over standard web protocols, chiefly HTTP.

The explanation

A socket is an endpoint of a communication channel. Each thread creates an endpoint object representing its end of the channel, and messages pass between the endpoints across the channel. The client thread's socket specifies a local I/O port to be used for sending messages — or the port can be chosen by the operating system — and it also carries the address of the destination machine and the port number expected to be bound to the server thread's socket. The server's socket specifies a local I/O port for receiving messages, and messages can be received from any client that knows both the server's machine address and the port bound to the server's socket. The client issues a request to form a connection, and once the server accepts it, messages pass in either direction. In Java the two classes are Socket and ServerSocket: the client creates a socket with the host and the server port, which requests the connection and throws an exception if it cannot connect; an input stream and an output stream are then taken from the socket so that reading and writing look like file I/O. The server creates one server socket and calls accept, which waits until a client requests a connection and returns a socket for that client, after which the server gets its streams, communicates, closes the connection and waits for the next request. A server can start a separate thread to handle each client. The operational fact to remember is blocking: a read on a socket's input stream normally blocks, a timeout can be set on the socket, and when it expires an exception is raised while the socket remains valid — a timeout means the peer did not answer in time, not that the channel is broken.

Web services exist to answer one problem: sharing data between programs that were never designed to cooperate. The clients, the database and the servers sit behind firewalls, routers and switches with security and compatibility constraints between them, and a direct connection between the database and the clients is normally not possible over the Internet because of firewalls and the risk of attack — while a direct connection inside a local network behind the firewall is normally fine. The solution is a web service: a standard way to get data over a network using standard web protocols, chiefly HTTP, which every browser, server and most programming languages support. It is not that HTTP is the best possible transport; it is what a firewall will let through. Formally, a web service is a method of communication between two devices over the World Wide Web, with standards defined by the W3C, and it is an API, cross-platform, implementable and usable in most programming languages, and built on standard web technology. Its popularity comes from easy data sharing over the Internet, platform-independent communication, integration of different systems and platforms, and distributed application development — which is to say that web services are Service Oriented Architecture in practice.

The two generations are told apart by their stacks, and only the top three layers change. Web Services 1.0 uses SOAP: WSDL describes the API in machine-readable form, SOAP wraps every message in an XML envelope, the payload is XML, and HTTP is the transport. Web Services 2.0 uses REST, which is less complex, lightweight and flexible and is the preferred model today: the payload is usually JSON with XML allowed, the meta-information rides in the HTTP headers instead of a wrapper, and there is often no machine-readable description at all, since WADL is completely optional and rarely used. The comparison itself has to be reproducible row by row. SOAP — full name Simple Object Access Protocol — envelopes the message: it runs on HTTP but wraps its own message inside the HTTP message, uses an XML-based data format, describes the API in WSDL, uses HTTP mainly as a transport with the operation named inside the SOAP body, is slower because of the envelope and XML processing, and is mature with a lot of functionality but not suitable for browser-based clients and more complicated to use. REST — Representational State Transfer — uses the HTTP headers to hold meta-information, expresses the operation and the resource through the method and the URL, uses the standard HTTP methods GET, PUT, POST and DELETE as the operations themselves, can be used with XML, JSON or whatever is necessary and usually JSON because it is easily parsable, describes the API in WADL which is optional, is faster than SOAP, and is lightweight and flexible. Three differences change how code is written — envelope against headers, XML only against JSON or XML, and a required description against an optional one — and two consequences follow: REST is faster and works in a browser, while SOAP is more mature and carries more functionality.

The worked architecture puts the pieces together: web server to web services to business logic to data source, split into a presentation layer, a logic layer and a foundations layer, installed on one or more servers in a local network or in the cloud. The presentation layer is the client — a browser, or another program calling the API. The logic layer holds the web service and the business logic behind it, and it is exposed to the world as an API. The foundations layer holds the data source and the server software, with the stored procedures living in the database rather than in the application. The sentence that matters is the last one: once the application tier is reachable as a web service over an ordinary HTTP connection, where it runs stops mattering.

How it runs

Two calls, side by side. A REST call is made of the HTTP method and the URL: the operation is the method, the resource is the path, and any meta-information rides in the headers, so the request is readable without a schema. A SOAP call carries the same intent inside an envelope — an XML body naming the operation, wrapped in the HTTP request — with WSDL on hand to say what the service accepts and returns. Both travel over the same transport, and both pass through the same firewall, which is the whole reason the design exists.

A socket conversation underneath them. The server opens a server socket on a port and calls accept, which blocks until a client asks for a connection. The client creates a socket naming the server's address and port, the connection is formed, and both sides take streams from their endpoints. The client writes a request and blocks on the read; the server reads it, computes an answer and writes back; the client's read returns. When the client closes the connection, the server goes back to accept for the next one — and each client can be handled by a thread of its own so that one slow conversation does not hold up the rest.

Exam traps

  • Sockets are the primitive, not an alternative to RPC. An answer that presents them as competing mechanisms misses the layering.
  • The client's socket holds three things — a local port, the destination address and the port bound at the server — while the server's holds a local port only, and it accepts whoever knows its address and port.
  • Web services exist because of firewalls. "Because HTTP is a standard" is half the answer; the reason HTTP was chosen is that it is what gets through.
  • The stacks are four layers thick and only the top three change: WSDL, SOAP and XML against WADL, REST and JSON, both on HTTP.
  • WSDL is required for SOAP and WADL is optional for REST. Reversing those two, or describing WADL as usual, loses the point of the comparison.
  • HTTP methods name the operation in REST and are only the transport in SOAP — that single row is the clearest way to explain the difference in style.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define a socket as an endpoint of a channel, then state what each end holds: the client's local port, destination address and server port; the server's local port.
  2. Give the four-step conversation — the client requests a connection, the server accepts, messages pass both ways, the connection closes — with the Java classes and streams as the concrete form.
  3. State that a read blocks and that a socket timeout leaves the socket valid.
  4. Give the reason web services exist: firewalls, and a database that cannot be reached directly over the Internet.
  5. Define a web service and list its properties — an API, cross-platform, most languages, standard web technology, W3C standards — then its benefits and its relationship to Service Oriented Architecture.
  6. Draw both four-layer stacks and say which three layers change.
  7. Reproduce the SOAP against REST comparison row by row: messaging, data format, API description, HTTP methods, speed, maturity and suitability, with an example tooling pair.
  8. Close with the worked architecture: the four parts, the three layers, and the statement that the tier stops mattering once it is reachable as a web service.
