3.0.html:
In one line

Time is the most important practical issue in distributed systems and the most problematic one: each computer has its own clock, so there is no single clock to read, and the clocks deviate and cannot be synchronized perfectly.

The explanation

Without global physical time it is hard to say what state one process is in while another is in a given state. Commerce still needs transactions timestamped consistently and an execution read as an order of events, so the problem cannot be avoided by ignoring it.

A computer timer is a counter register and a holding register decremented by a quartz crystal oscillator and reloaded at zero; each interrupt is a clock tick, and the resulting physical clock counts oscillations at a definite frequency. The drift rate — how fast a clock deviates from real time — is what decides how often it must be synchronized, and a synchronized clock is one that does not deviate from real time by more than a certain amount. Time is needed for performance measurement, for judging whether data is recent, for temporal ordering, for sender and receiver synchronization, for shared access to resources.

The classical failure caused by unsynchronized clocks is make, which uses the clock of the machine it runs on to decide which source files need recompiling. With the sources on a separate file server and the clocks unsynchronized, the output can be judged newer than its source, and a rebuild that was needed is skipped. The general statement is the one to remember: an event that occurred after another may be assigned an earlier time, and that is a correctness problem rather than a performance problem.

With no common memory and no common clock, two events sometimes cannot be ordered by measurement, so order is defined without time. The happened-before relation is a partial ordering built from three rules: events within one process are ordered; a send happens before its receive; and the relation is transitive. Events not related by it are concurrent — there is no causal relationship between them at all. A global order can be built from timestamps in one direction only: if an event happens before another, its timestamp is smaller, but a smaller timestamp does not prove that the event happened first.

Causal ordering of messages is the practical consequence. If one message is sent before another, every recipient of both must receive the first before the second — and the network does not promise that, because a message can take a different route and overtake an earlier one. In a replicated database, updates received out of order make the replicas diverge. The fix is to buffer a later message until the earlier one it depends on has been delivered, and to decide whether a message is later than one still awaited a Lamport timestamp is not enough, because it cannot decide dependency. A vector timestamp can.

How it runs

A short exchange, with the clocks disagreeing. One process writes a file on a file server and another process, moments later, compiles it. Each machine stamps its work with its own clock, and the two clocks have drifted apart by more than the interval between the operations.

The compile can therefore see an object file whose timestamp is later than the file it was built from, decide the object is current, and skip the rebuild — while the change to that file is real and the binary is stale. Nothing failed, no message was lost, and the system is still wrong, because the comparison of two timestamps from two unsynchronized clocks carried no information.

Now put two messages in flight between the same pair of processes. The second is sent after the first, takes a shorter route, and arrives before it. Every process that holds both has seen the newer update first, and if the messages are updates to a replica, the replica now records the older value as the newer one. Buffering the second until the first arrives is the repair, and it needs a timestamp that can say the first message is a dependency of the second — which is exactly what a vector clock carries and a Lamport timestamp does not.

Exam traps

  • The make example is asked for as a worked illustration, not as a name. The answer needs the mechanism — the object judged newer than its source — and the statement that it is a correctness problem.
  • The happened-before relation is a partial order defined by three rules, and events outside it are concurrent. It is defined without reference to clocks, and answering it with timestamps reverses the logic.
  • Timestamps give a one-directional implication. If one event happens before another its timestamp is smaller, but the converse does not hold; that limitation is the reason vector clocks exist.
  • Drift rate is why synchronization has to be repeated at a chosen interval, and a synchronized clock is defined by a bound on deviation.
  • Buffering is the mechanism for causal ordering. Saying "the network delivers in order" contradicts the reason the topic exists.

Full-marks answer

  1. State why time is both the most important and the most problematic practical issue, with the drift and the absence of a single clock.
  2. Describe the timer hardware — counter register, holding register, oscillator, tick — and define drift rate and a synchronized clock.
  3. Work the make example through, then state the general failure it illustrates.
  4. Define the happened-before relation by its three rules, define concurrency, and explain how a global order is built from timestamps and why the implication runs one way only.
  5. Set out causal ordering of messages: the requirement, the overtaking problem, the divergence it causes in a replicated database, and buffering as the fix.
  6. Close by naming which timestamp can decide dependency and which cannot.

3.1.html:
In one line

Clock synchronization splits into two families — physical clock synchronization, which moves the clocks themselves toward real time, and logical clock synchronization, which orders events without claiming to know the time — and the physical family is Cristian's algorithm for a centralized system and the Network Time Protocol for a distributed one.

The explanation

Cristian's algorithm relies on a time server whose clock comes from a radio clock or another accurate source of UTC. The client requests the time; the server replies with the time T from its own clock appended; the client sets its clock to T + RTT/2, where RTT is the round-trip time of the request. Both timestamps are taken from the client's clock, and the one-way delay is assumed to be half the round trip, so the accuracy is half the round trip. The interrupt handling time is a third quantity to subtract if it is being counted.

The assumption underneath is that the round trip is split equally between the request and the response, which is reasonable on a LAN connection, and accuracy improves by making multiple requests and keeping the answer with the shortest round trip. Formally, if the minimum one-way transmission time is known, the server's time when the reply arrives lies between the server's timestamp plus that minimum and the server's timestamp plus the round trip minus that minimum; the width of that range is the round trip minus twice the minimum, giving an accuracy of half the round trip minus the minimum. The server must not jump: it changes its time gradually, by slewing the clock rather than setting it, so that time never goes backwards for the programs reading it.

NTP is the most commonly used internet time protocol and the one with the best accuracy. Clients take updates from one or more servers and average them; the simplified version that skips the statistical work is SNTP. Servers listen on port 123 and reply with a UDP packet carrying a 64-bit timestamp in UTC seconds counted from 1 January 1900. Time sources form a synchronization subnet of strata: the first stratum connects directly to an accurate source, and each stratum beneath it is synchronized from the one above it.

NTP's goals are accuracy to UTC despite message delays, filtering by statistics, reliable service, frequent synchronization and authentication. It has three synchronization modes, and they trade accuracy against cost. Multicast mode is low accuracy, for quick LANs, and the server periodically multicasts its time to the clients in its subnet. Remote procedure call mode is medium accuracy: the server replies to each request with its actual timestamp. Symmetric mode is high accuracy and is used to synchronize between the time servers themselves, peer to peer. All three are delivered unreliably over UDP, which is why the protocol needs many rounds and statistical filtering to reach its accuracy.

The offset derivation is the part of NTP that is examined as arithmetic, and it needs four timestamps: when the client sends, when the server receives, when the server responds, and when the client receives the response. The client can measure the last minus the first from its own clock, and the server reports the middle two. Total transit time is therefore the elapsed time minus the time the server spent working, and with that transit time split equally between the two legs, the offset is half the sum of the forward leg and the backward leg. Without subtracting the server's processing time, that working time would be counted as network delay and the estimate would be wrong by it.

How it runs

Follow one NTP exchange. The client writes its own clock into the first timestamp and sends the request; the server stamps its own clock on arrival and again on departure, and replies with both values; the client stamps its own clock when the reply arrives.

The client now holds four numbers, two of its own and two from the server. The difference between its two timestamps is the total time the exchange took, and the difference between the server's two is the time the server spent working on it. Subtracting the second from the first leaves the time actually spent in transit, in both directions.

With the transit split equally — the assumption the whole estimate rests on — the client's clock offset is half the sum of the forward and backward legs, and it applies that offset gradually rather than jumping. Several such exchanges are usually run and the result is filtered, because a single round trip may have been delayed anywhere along the path. That statistical filtering, plus authentication, is what separates NTP from a single request and reply.

Exam traps

  • Cristian's accuracy comes from the assumption that the round trip is split equally. State the assumption, then the accuracy in terms of the round trip.
  • The server slews rather than sets. Gradual adjustment is the answer to the problem of a clock jumping backwards.
  • The four timestamps and the offset formula are asked for as a derivation. Writing only the final formula loses the marks for the transit time and for the server's processing time.
  • The three NTP modes are multicast, remote procedure call and symmetric, in ascending order of accuracy, with the peer-to-peer one used between servers.
  • Port 123, UDP, and the timestamp counted in seconds from 1 January 1900 are the fixed details of NTP that are quoted in questions about it.
  • Stratum one connects directly to an accurate source and each stratum below is synchronized from the one above — not the other way round.

Full-marks answer

  1. Split clock synchronization into the physical and logical families, and name the two algorithms of the physical family.
  2. Cristian's algorithm: the time server and its UTC source, the request and reply, the clock set to the server's time plus half the round trip, and the accuracy that follows.
  3. The refinement: several requests, the shortest round trip kept, the range the server's time lies in, and slewing instead of setting.
  4. NTP: the clients and averaging, SNTP as the simplified form, the port and packet, the timestamp and its epoch, and the synchronization subnet of strata.
  5. NTP's goals, then its three modes with the accuracy each buys.
  6. Derive the offset from the four timestamps, explain why the server's processing time must be subtracted, and close on why the round trip is split equally.
points: The client requests the time, the server replies with its clock, and the client sets its clock to the server's time plus half the round trip.
Half the round trip, on the assumption that the round trip is split equally between the request and the response.
The server changes its time gradually rather than setting it, so time never goes backwards for the programs reading it.
The most commonly used internet time protocol and the most accurate, with clients averaging updates from several servers.
Time sources form a synchronisation subnet: the first stratum connects directly to an accurate source, and each stratum beneath it is synchronised from the one above.
Multicast is low accuracy, remote procedure call is medium, and symmetric mode is high accuracy between the time servers themselves.
From four timestamps the client derives its offset, subtracting the server's working time so it is not counted as network delay.

3.2.t: Logical Clocks: Lamport's and Vector Clocks
3.2.html:
In one line

A logical clock is a monotonically increasing software counter whose value need bear no particular relationship to any physical clock, used to give events a consistent order; Lamport timestamps give a total order consistent with causality, and vector clocks are the extension that can decide whether two events are causally related or concurrent.

The explanation

Clock synchronization minimizes the difference between accepted actual time and the time on a client machine, and even then relying on local clock time stays risky: a recorded time may have happened at a different time on another computer, because the drift rates differ. Correcting the clocks means the machines are much closer to each other on average, not that they all agree on time. A logical clock steps around that: each process keeps its own counter and uses it to apply timestamps to events, giving consistent event ordering without needing the clocks to agree. The counters only have to be internally consistent, and logical clocks live in the middleware layer, which timestamps on send and updates on receipt, so the application never touches a clock.

A Lamport logical clock is an incrementing counter per process with three rules. A process increments its counter before each event in that process. On sending, the value travels with the message. On receiving, the counter is set above the maximum of its own value and the received one. The result is a total order over all events, which is enough to order concurrent requests for a single resource.

Four considerations limit what that order means. Within a process no two events may share a timestamp, and a unique process identifier may be needed to tell simultaneous events apart. A system has partial order when a partial-order relationship exists among its events and total order when causality relates them all. In replicated systems an update is timestamped at its accepting site and ordered by source timestamp at the receiver. And the limitation that everything else follows from: Lamport clocks give a total order consistent with causality, but a smaller timestamp does not imply that the event happened first, because concurrent events can carry any two values.

A vector clock is an array of logical clocks, one per process, which detects causality violations. The entry for a site at any moment is the most recent value of that site's clock the holder has heard about. An internal event increments the process's own entry; a send increments it and sends the whole vector; a receive increments it again and takes the pairwise maximum with the received vector. Two events are causally related exactly when one vector dominates the other, and non-dominating vectors are provably concurrent. That is the property a scalar timestamp cannot have.

Causal ordering using these clocks keeps the causal order of receives the same as the order of sends, and two named algorithms do it: one for causal ordering of broadcasts, and one for causal ordering of regular messages, both delaying an out-of-order message until the messages it depends on have been delivered. The reason a vector timestamp is required is exactly the decision rule mentioned earlier: to delay a message, a process has to decide whether it is later than one it is still awaiting, and a Lamport timestamp cannot answer that question, while a vector timestamp can — one message causally precedes another exactly when its vector is dominated by the other's.

How it runs

Two processes and three events, followed through the counters. The first process performs an internal event, so it increments its own counter; it then sends a message, so it increments again and attaches the value. The second process receives it, compares the received value with its own, and sets its counter above the larger of the two — after which any event it performs carries a value larger than the message it just received.

Now suppose the first process performs another internal event without sending anything. Its counter moves ahead, but the second process hears nothing, so the two counters advance independently. Comparing the two numbers at that moment cannot say whether the second process's event preceded or followed the first's: they are concurrent, and both orders of the two numbers are consistent with the messages that actually happened.

Carry the same sequence with vectors instead. The send attaches the whole array, and the receive takes the pairwise maximum, so each process's array describes how much of every other process's history it has seen. The earlier event's array is dominated by the later one's along every entry, and the two concurrent events have entries in which each is ahead of the other — which is the definition of concurrency, decided rather than guessed.

Exam traps

  • The Lamport algorithm is three rules — increment before each event, send the value with the message, on receipt take the maximum and exceed it. The third rule is where answers usually go vague.
  • State the limitation explicitly: a smaller timestamp does not imply that the event happened first.
  • Vector clocks are arrays with one entry per process, and both the send and the receive rule apply to the whole array. Describing them as "a better Lamport clock" earns nothing.
  • Dominance is the test for causality and non-dominance is the proof of concurrency. Both halves are needed.
  • The reason vector clocks exist is the decision a delayed message needs: whether a message being held is later than one still awaited.
  • Logical clocks are described as living in the middleware, timestamping on send and updating on receipt, which is what keeps the application out of it.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define a logical clock and say why it is enough for ordering even though it need not track real time.
  2. Give the three rules of a Lamport clock, then the total order it produces and what that order is good for.
  3. Give the four considerations: uniqueness within a process, partial against total order, the replicated-system rule, and the one-directional limitation.
  4. Define a vector clock as an array with one entry per process, and give the internal, send and receive rules.
  5. State the causality test — one vector dominates the other — and that non-dominating vectors are provably concurrent.
  6. Explain causal ordering: what has to be preserved, the two named algorithms, the buffering they perform, and why a vector timestamp rather than a Lamport one is required.

3.3.html:
In one line

Mutual exclusion is the property that only one process enters a critical section at a time; permission-based algorithms arbitrate by asking permission from the other processes, and token-based algorithms pass a single token that carries the right to enter.

The explanation

Mutual exclusion is needed only where processes must exchange information to reach agreement. One-way communication usually does not need it, and in client/server communication the server handles the coordination, so the clients never interact. A critical section is a region where a process competes destructively with another for a shared item, a race condition comes from two processes entering that region at the same time, and mutual exclusion is the solution.

The requirements come in two groups, and this is the part examiners separate carefully. Safety, liveness, no starvation and fairness. Safety says at most one process is in the critical section — what must never happen. Liveness says that if more than one process is requesting, someone enters. No starvation says a requesting process enters within a finite time. Fairness says requests are granted in order, which implies both no starvation and liveness. Three of the four are claims about progress, and one is a prohibition; keeping them apart is most of the answer.

Two families answer the question of who may enter. Permission-based algorithms let every process compete freely, and the requests are arbitrated either by a central coordinator or by distributed agreement; the named algorithms are a central coordinator, Lamport's, Ricart–Agrawala and the Token Ring. Token-based algorithms give the right to enter to whoever holds a single token. The trade is the usual one: asking first costs messages and usually a wait when something fails, while holding a token costs nothing to use but the token must be found and regenerated when it is lost.

Ricart–Agrawala improves on Lamport's algorithm in one decisive respect: a node need not send a reply when it holds a request with a lower timestamp, so the reply is deferred rather than sent and then made irrelevant. No FIFO channels are required, because the ordering is carried in the timestamps themselves rather than in the order the messages happen to arrive. The cost is two messages for every other node per entry into the critical section — a request to every other node and a reply from every other node. Requests are granted in order of increasing timestamps, the synchronization delay is the maximum transmission time, and a node enters on replies from all the others and then replies to the requests it deferred.

The Token Ring is the token family's standard example. A single token circulates and whoever holds it may enter the critical section. The processes form a logical ring, each holding the address of one neighbour, and a process waits for the token from its left neighbour and then passes it on clockwise. Obtaining the token can take from one message to almost a full lap, with the worst case being a full lap, and the algorithm behaves well when the system is heavily loaded, because the token is passed whether or not anyone wants it. Its weakness is stated in one line: if the holder fails, a unique process must be elected to regenerate the token — which is where leader election comes in.

How it runs

A Ricart–Agrawala entry, message by message. A node that wants the critical section sends a request carrying its timestamp to every other node, and waits. Each node that receives the request replies at once if it is not interested in the critical section and is not waiting on an earlier request; if it is holding a request with a lower timestamp, it defers the reply and remembers the requester.

Replies arrive from all the others, the node enters, does its work, and on leaving sends the deferred replies to everyone it had held back. Because the decision is taken from timestamps and not from the order in which the requests happened to arrive, the channels carrying them need no ordering guarantee — which is the improvement over the algorithm it replaced.

Now the token ring, in the same terms. A single token circulates clockwise; a node that wants to enter simply waits for it rather than sending anything. If nobody wants to enter, the token still travels, so the load does not change the traffic. When the token holder fails, the ring has no token at all, and nothing in the protocol can produce one: a unique process has to be elected and made responsible for generating it again, which is why election is a companion topic rather than a separate one.

Exam traps

  • Safety, liveness, no starvation and fairness are the four requirements, and they must be grouped as one prohibition and three progress claims. Fairness implies the other two progress claims, and saying so earns a mark.
  • Ricart–Agrawala's advantage is the deferred reply when a lower timestamp is held, not merely the use of timestamps.
  • The message cost is counted per critical-section entry: a request to every other node and a reply from every other node. Answers that give only one of the two halves understate it.
  • No FIFO channels are needed in Ricart–Agrawala, because the ordering rides in the timestamps. That is the point of naming it as an improvement.
  • The Token Ring's cost is expressed as the number of messages to obtain the token, with the worst case a full lap, and its behaviour improves under heavy load rather than degrading.
  • The failure answer for a token algorithm is election plus regeneration of the token. "The token is recreated" without the election omits the mechanism.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define mutual exclusion, the critical section and the race condition, and note when mutual exclusion is needed at all.
  2. Give the four requirements, grouped into the safety property and the three progress properties, with the implication between fairness and the other two.
  3. Name the two families and place the four algorithms in them: central coordinator, Lamport's, Ricart–Agrawala and the Token Ring.
  4. Set out Ricart–Agrawala: the request with a timestamp to every node, the immediate or deferred reply, the entry on replies from all, the replies sent after leaving, the message cost and the absence of a channel-ordering requirement.
  5. Set out the Token Ring: the circulating token, the logical ring of neighbours, the clockwise pass, the cost in messages and the heavy-load behaviour.
  6. Close by naming the failure of each family — a wait on failure for permission-based, and the lost token that has to be regenerated after an election for token-based.

Requests are granted in order, which implies both liveness and no starvation.

3.4.html:
In one line

Leader election designates one process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes: before it runs no node knows who will lead, and afterwards every node recognizes the same unique leader.

The explanation

Election is needed at the initialization of a central coordinator, whenever that coordinator crashes, and in the token ring when the token holder fails. It also selects the master that takes responsibility for averaging the time in the Berkeley algorithm, and it is what a distributed algorithm needs when no coordinator exists and one process must distribute sub-problems and collect the partial results.

The scheme rests on a unique priority number associated with each active process, with the coordinator always the process having the largest priority number. When the coordinator fails, the active process with the largest priority number is elected, and a crashed node cannot win because it cannot take part. The requirement is that one and only one process is chosen and that all agree on the decision, and the election starts after a failure, which is normally detected by a time-out. There are two phases: select the leader with the highest priority, then inform all processes of the winner.

The Bully algorithm elects the active process with the largest process identifier where every process can reach every other. It uses three messages: an election message, an answer that a process is alive, and a coordinator message naming the winner. A process that finds the coordinator down messages every process with a higher identifier, and elects itself if none answers within its time-out. If a higher process answers, the caller waits for that process to announce itself and restarts the election if nothing arrives. The behaviour that gives the algorithm its name is at the end: a process with a high number that recovers runs the algorithm at once and bullies a lower-numbered coordinator out of the role.

The Ring algorithm, due to Chang and Roberts, elects the largest identification in a logical or physical ring. It works for any number of processes, and no process needs to know the size of the ring. A process that notices the lack of a leader sends an election message carrying its own unique identifier to its neighbour clockwise. On receiving one, a process forwards it if it carries a larger identifier and replaces a smaller one that it has not already forwarded. When an identifier returns to the process that originated it, that process is the leader, and it sends an elected message round the ring.

The comparison is the part that has to be reproducible. The two algorithms agree on who wins — the largest identifier — and differ in what they assume and what they cost. Bully assumes every process can message every other, a mesh for example, while the ring assumes only a unidirectional link to the next neighbour. Bully sends election messages to every higher-numbered process, collects the answers from the living, and then broadcasts the victory; the ring spends one election message that accumulates identifiers and one coordinator message, two laps in the normal case. Bully needs each process to know the higher numbers in the ring of members, while the ring works for any number of processes without that knowledge.

How it runs

The Bully algorithm in action. A process notices that the coordinator has stopped answering, and sends an election message to every process with a higher identifier than its own. Each of those answers that it is alive; then, because a higher process exists, the caller stops and waits for one of them to announce itself as coordinator.

One of the higher processes does the same thing in turn, and the process with the highest identifier of all eventually receives no answer at all. It declares itself the coordinator, sends the coordinator message to every process, and the election ends with everyone agreeing on the same winner. If a process with an even higher identifier was down and now recovers, it runs the election on its own initiative and takes the role from the incumbent — the winner is the largest identifier that is currently alive, not the one that won last time.

The ring algorithm in the same terms. A process that finds no leader sends its own identifier clockwise. Each neighbour compares the arriving identifier with its own and passes on the larger, or passes on the arriving one if its own is smaller and it has not already sent that message. Every identifier that survives a lap belongs to the process with the largest identifier, which recognises its own value coming back, declares itself elected, and sends the elected message round the ring so the others can record the result.

Exam traps

  • Election has two phases — selecting the highest priority and informing everyone — and the second phase is what makes the winner unique for all nodes.
  • A crashed node cannot win, and the largest priority among the active processes is what is being elected. That qualifier is worth writing.
  • Bully's three messages must be named: election, answer, coordinator.
  • The name Bully explains the behaviour after recovery, where a high-numbered process runs the election at once. An answer that treats the name as decoration misses the mark.
  • The ring works for any number of processes and needs no process to know the ring size; Bully needs every process to be able to reach every other.
  • Both algorithms elect the largest identifier, so the comparison must be about assumptions and messages, not about who wins.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define leader election and the two states of knowledge — before and after the algorithm runs.
  2. State where it is needed: the initialization of a central coordinator, the recovery of a failed coordinator, the token ring's lost token, and the Berkeley averaging master.
  3. Give the priority-number scheme, the largest-priority rule, the one-and-only-one requirement, the time-out that starts it, and the two phases.
  4. Describe Bully with its assumption, its three messages, the time-out behaviour, the recovery behaviour, and the number of messages it costs.
  5. Describe the Chang and Roberts ring with its assumption, the clockwise election message, the replace-a-smaller-identifier rule, the originator's recognition, and the elected message.
  6. Close with the comparison: same winner, different assumptions, different message counts, different prerequisites.
points: Each active process has a unique priority, and the coordinator is always the process with the largest — so a crashed node cannot win.
Select the leader with the highest priority, then inform all processes of the winner.
Where every process can reach every other, a process finding the coordinator down messages every higher identifier and elects itself if none answers.
An election message, an answer that a process is alive, and a coordinator message naming the winner.
A high-numbered process that recovers runs the algorithm at once and bullies a lower-numbered coordinator out of the role.
The ring algorithm elects the largest identification and works for any number of processes, with no process knowing the ring size.
The same winner, different assumptions: a mesh against unidirectional links, and election messages to every higher number against a message that accumulates identifiers.

4.1.t: DFS concepts: Transparency, Naming, Replication, Consistency
4.1.html:
In one line

A Distributed File System is a classical file system spread across multiple machines, sharing dispersed files, so that programs store and access remote files exactly as they do local ones.

The explanation

The definitions matter because they fix the standard being aimed at. Resources on another machine are remote; resources on the local machine are local. The requirement is that programs can store and access remote files exactly as they do local ones, and that clients view the system the same way they view a centralized file system, with the distribution hidden at a lower level. Performance is judged by two numbers: throughput and response time.

Eight concepts, requirements and design goals apply. Transparency: the distribution is invisible and remote files are used as local ones. Concurrency, replication, heterogeneity and fault tolerance. Consistency: all readers see updates according to a defined rule, despite caching and replication. Security, applying to remote files as strictly as to local ones; and efficiency, meaning throughput and response time close to those of a local file system.

Transparency in a DFS is the family of properties applied to files. Its strict form is access transparency: the same operations on a remote file as on a local one, with the same result. The others are location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure and persistence. NFS is described as having access transparency as its design goal, where most other systems have something else, and that one sentence is the clearest way to place it.

Naming maps logical objects to physical ones, and the three schemes differ in how much location transparency they give. Host plus local name is unique but neither location transparent nor location independent. Remote directories mounted to local ones is location independent, but the directories must be explicitly mounted — SUN NFS is the example. A single global name structure spans all files and gives the strongest illusion of one system. Underneath any of them sits a transparent mapping from name to file_identifier to a triple of system, disk, cylinder and sector, which is what allows a file to be moved without changing its name: the identifier changes, the name does not.

The file service architecture structures the system into three components. The flat file service acts on the contents of files, referring to them by UFID. The directory service maps text names to those identifiers and supports creating directories and adding files. The client module runs on each computer and gives applications a single API over both services; it holds the network locations of the servers and caches recently used file blocks.

Consistency is the requirement that all clients see the effects of updates by a defined rule when a file is replicated or cached, and it is unavoidable: caching is mandatory for performance, replication for availability, and concurrent access is normal. Two ends of the range are named. Strict consistency is that every read sees the most recent write at once. Relaxed consistency is that staleness is bounded by a rule rather than eliminated. NFS chooses relaxed consistency in the close-to-open form, with a consistency window of 30 seconds.

Replication means multiple copies of a file, and a transparent DFS returns a set of locations for the replicas rather than one. It has three motivations. Availability and fault tolerance: if one server or disk fails, another copy answers, which is the purpose it serves in HDFS. Read performance: a read can be served by the nearest or least-loaded replica. Bandwidth: copies can be placed near the readers. The price is consistency, and the systems differ in how much of it they take: minimal replication in NFS, read-one and write-all in Coda, none at all in Plan 9, and striping for bandwidth in xFS.

How it runs

A file open, followed through the components. An application calls the client module on its own machine with a text name. The client module asks the directory service for that name, and the directory service returns the file identifier it maps to; the application never sees the identifier, which is why the name is what a program and its users deal with.

The client module then uses that identifier against the flat file service, whose server may be on another machine entirely. The server acts on the file contents and returns the data, and the client module caches the blocks it has just read so the next open of the same file does not repeat the round trip. Only the client module knows that the server is remote; the two services and the application are written as though all of it were local.

Now open the same file on a second machine while a write is in flight from the first. The second machine may hold a cached block that the write has invalidated, and what it sees depends entirely on the consistency rule chosen rather than on the code. Under close-to-open with a bounded staleness window, the second reader is guaranteed to see the earlier writer's changes only when it opens the file after the window has passed — and everything between those two moments is a deliberately bounded approximation.

Exam traps

  • The eight concepts are asked for as a group: transparency, concurrency, replication, heterogeneity, fault tolerance, consistency, security, efficiency. Listing only transparency and consistency is a half answer.
  • Access transparency is the strict form, and it is the one NFS is built around. The other transparencies are the familiar family from distributed systems in general.
  • The naming schemes are compared by location transparency and location independence — host plus name is neither, mounted remote directories are location independent, and a global name structure is the strongest.
  • The mapping underneath naming is the reason a file can move without its name changing, and the answer should say which part of the triple changes.
  • UFID belongs to the flat file service and text names to the directory service. Swapping them is the commonest error in this topic.
  • Strict and relaxed consistency are the two ends, with NFS's close-to-open window as the named middle. Replication's three motivations are availability, read performance and bandwidth, with consistency as the price of the first.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define a DFS and the local and remote distinction, and give the two performance measures.
  2. List the eight concepts and design goals with a clause each.
  3. Give transparency's family, marking access transparency as the strict form and NFS's goal.
  4. Give the three naming schemes with what each buys, then the transparent mapping from name to file identifier to physical location.
  5. Describe the file service architecture: flat file service with UFIDs, directory service mapping names, client module giving one API and caching.
  6. Explain why consistency is unavoidable, give strict and relaxed as the ends, and place NFS's close-to-open window on the scale.
  7. Close with replication: the set of locations, the three motivations, and the consistency price.
points: The same operations on a remote file as on a local one, with the same result — the strict form, and NFS's design goal.
Host plus local name, remote directories mounted to local ones, or a single global name structure spanning all files.
Name to file identifier to a triple of system, disk, cylinder and sector, so a file can be moved without its name changing.
A flat file service acting on UFIDs, a directory service mapping text names to them, and a client module giving one API and caching blocks.
All readers see updates by a defined rule: strict consistency at one end and relaxed consistency at the other.
NFS's relaxed rule, with a consistency window of 30 seconds.
Multiple copies with a set of locations returned; the motivations are availability, read performance and bandwidth.

4.2.html:
In one line

SUN NFS is the network file system that made transparent file sharing a standard — stateless, built on remote procedure calls — and HDFS is the file system for very large files on commodity hardware, with a single master holding the metadata and workers holding replicated blocks.

The explanation

SUN NFS was developed by Sun Microsystems in 1985 and was the first commercially successful network file system. It was developed for diskless workstations and designed for robustness and adequate performance rather than the best possible performance. Sun published all the protocol specifications, which is why NFS became a standard rather than a product. It is both an implementation and a specification, its goal is to share a file system transparently, and it uses the client-server model although a node can be both client and server at once and there is no dedicated server.

Its most consequential decision is that it is stateless: every client request provides the complete information the server needs. A stateful server keeps track of client requests — which files are open, connection identifiers, caches — and performs better, because the file name is not parsed on every request. A stateless server has nothing to reclaim or lose after a failure, so it recovers easily and the client simply retries; the cost is that every request repeats the lookup, which is why client caching has to compensate.

NFS's design has three parts. The protocol uses the Sun RPC mechanism and the Sun eXternal Data Representation, defined as a set of remote procedures. The server side identifies files by a file handle holding a filesystem identifier, an i-node number and a generation number. The client side gives a transparent interface, where a remote mount maps remote names to addresses and the virtual file system and vnode calls carry the operations. Because the server is stateless, identity and access rights are checked on every request, which carries the user identifier and group identifier with it.

HDFS is the other extreme in the same family. It stores very large files with streaming data access on clusters of commodity hardware. Very large files means hundreds of megabytes to terabytes in a file, with clusters holding petabytes. Streaming access means the pattern is write-once, read-many-times — a dataset generated once and then analysed many times. Commodity hardware means node failure is expected, and HDFS carries on without a noticeable interruption. It is a poor fit for low-latency data access, for a great many small files, and for multiple writers.

Its unit is the block, much larger than in a conventional file system: 64 MB by default, often 128 MB. Files are broken into block-sized chunks stored as independent units, so a file can be larger than any single disk, and the storage subsystem deals with blocks rather than files, which removes a whole class of metadata concerns. Blocks are what replication acts on, and each is replicated to a small number of separate machines, typically three. The size is chosen to minimise the cost of seeks: the arithmetic is that a seek costs about 10 ms against a transfer rate of about 100 MB/s, so a block near 100 MB keeps the transfer time well above the seek time.

The architecture is a namenode as master and datanodes as workers. The namenode manages the filesystem namespace — the tree and the metadata for all files and directories — and it knows which datanodes hold every block, while the data itself never passes through it. Its metadata is persisted as two files, a namespace image and an edit log. Datanodes store and retrieve blocks when they are told to and report the blocks they hold periodically. A Secondary NameNode takes snapshots, which is what keeps the namespace image and the edit log from growing without bound.

The namenode is a single point of failure, and the remedies are a named list. Backing up the state: the namenode writes its persistent state to multiple file systems, synchronously and atomically. The secondary namenode merges the namespace image with the edit log periodically — it does not act as a namenode. HDFS Federation adds namenodes, each managing a portion of the namespace, which do not communicate with each other although datanodes register with all of them. High availability is the fourth answer: a pair of namenodes running active and standby, so the standby takes over without significant interruption, which needs shared storage for the edit log, reporting to both namenodes, client failover, a failover controller to manage the transition, and fencing to make an ungraceful failover safe. Recovery the old way is a cold start that can take 30 minutes or more on a large cluster, which is the measure of what that machinery buys.

HDFS was inspired by GFS, the Google File System, and the assumptions behind both are the same four: hardware failures are common, files are large and few, writes append rather than rewrite, and high sustained bandwidth is preferred to low latency. GFS's shape is a single master holding metadata and many chunkservers holding fixed-size chunks with three replicas. The read path is worth following: the client asks the master for the chunk handle and the replica locations, caches them, and then asks the closest replica directly.

How it runs

A read of a large file in HDFS, step by step. The client asks the namenode for the blocks of the file, and the namenode answers with the location of each block's replicas — the data does not travel through the namenode, so the master is consulted once per file rather than once per byte.

The client caches those locations and reads each block from the nearest replica, so a second read of the same block within the same session does not repeat the lookup. Meanwhile the datanode that holds the block reads it from its local disk and streams it back, and other datanodes holding the same block are simply idle for this read — which is what makes the failure of one of them invisible.

Now kill a datanode that holds a block the client wants. The namenode notices the periodic reports stop, records the block's remaining replicas, and the next read is served from one of them. Nothing in the client's read path changes, and nothing had to be restarted to make it work, which is the availability that replication buys: the failure costs a replica rather than an operation.

Exam traps

  • Statelessness is NFS's central decision, and the answer should give both sides: easy recovery and no state to reclaim against repeating the lookup on every request.
  • The file handle has three parts — filesystem identifier, i-node number, generation number — and the stateless server checks identity and access rights on every request.
  • HDFS's block size is given with its reason. The seek against transfer arithmetic is the reason, not the number on its own.
  • The namenode holds metadata only; the data never passes through it. Datanodes report the blocks they hold periodically.
  • The Secondary NameNode is not a standby and takes no failover. It merges the namespace image with the edit log, and its name is the trap in this topic.
  • The namenode being a single point of failure has four named remedies — state backed up to several file systems, the secondary namenode's merges, HDFS Federation, and the active-standby pair with a failover controller and fencing. High availability needs shared storage for the edit log.

Full-marks answer

  1. Place SUN NFS by its origin, its diskless-workstation motivation, its published specification, and its client-server shape with no dedicated server.
  2. Explain statelessness and the stateful alternative, with the costs and benefits of each.
  3. Give NFS's three parts: the protocol on Sun RPC with external data representation, the server's file handle and its three components, and the client's transparent interface with mounting.
  4. Introduce HDFS by its three assumptions and the workloads it fits poorly.
  5. Give the block, its default and common sizes, the reason for its size, and its replication factor.
  6. Describe the namenode and datanodes, the namespace and the two metadata files, and the secondary namenode's merging role.
  7. Work through the single point of failure and the four remedies, ending with high availability: the active-standby pair, shared edit log storage, client failover, the failover controller and fencing.
  8. Close with GFS: the four shared assumptions, the master and chunkserver shape, and the read path with the cached replica locations.

Very large files with streaming data access on clusters of commodity hardware, where node failure is expected.
64 MB by default and often 128 MB: a seek costs about 10 ms against a transfer rate of about 100 MB/s.

4.3.t: Middleware: CORBA, Java RMI, Messaging MQTT, AMQP
4.3.html:
In one line

Middleware is a set of services that enables applications and end users to interact across a heterogeneous distributed system, sitting above the network and below the application software, and the three families are object-based middleware such as CORBA and Java RMI, and message-oriented middleware such as MQTT and AMQP.

The explanation

Distributed applications are typically heterogeneous: different hardware, different software, unconventional devices, and diverse networks and protocols. It happens for three reasons — different solutions suit different parts of an application, users choose their own vendors, and legacy systems have to keep working. Middleware's two jobs are to make the network transparent to users and applications, and to hide the hardware, operating system and software details.

CORBA is the Object Management Group's specification for an Object Request Broker. It is a standard rather than a product, and it is language-neutral and vendor-neutral, with everything defined by an IDL. Clients invoke through proxies and servers through skeletons, both generated from the IDL, which is what lets a client written in one language call a server written in another. The interface repository holds the available interfaces, and that is what makes dynamic invocation possible — a client can discover an interface it was not compiled against. GIOP defines the messages exchanged between object request brokers, and IIOP is its particularisation over TCP/IP. Its services include naming and trading, security, time, event and notification, transaction, and persistent objects.

Java RMI is language-specific middleware, and the comparison with CORBA is the point of putting the two side by side: CORBA's interface is defined in a neutral language, while RMI's interface is the implementation language itself. RMI extends the Java object model to support distributed objects, letting objects invoke methods on remote objects with local syntax; type checking applies equally to remote and local calls, and a binder maps textual names to remote object references. Its cost is that it is a single-language system, which is not enough in a heterogeneous estate — the estate that middleware exists for.

The third family is message-oriented middleware, where the unit of interaction is a message rather than a method call, and MQTT, AMQP, CoAP and XMPP are the names to carry. MQTT is publish-subscribe messaging for lightweight devices over unreliable networks or intermittent connectivity, which is why it is popular for IoT and machine-to-machine work. The publisher never names a receiver: a broker forwards data to interested subscribers, and the topic decouples them, so neither side needs to know the other exists or be running at the same time. Its overhead is deliberately small — a one-byte control header and a one-to-four-byte packet length, then an optional variable header and payload — and that frugality is what makes it usable on constrained devices. AMQP is a binary application-layer protocol for machine-to-machine messaging, supporting both publish-subscribe and request-response, with queues and exchanges as the mechanism that routes messages from senders to receivers.

How it runs

A CORBA call, from the client's point of view. The client holds a proxy generated from the interface definition in the IDL, and calling a method on it looks like a local call in the client's own language. The proxy marshals the arguments and hands the request to the object request broker, which is the piece that knows where the servant object lives; the broker's messages to its peers follow the general inter-ORB protocol, which over TCP/IP is its internet specialisation.

On the server side, the skeleton generated from the same IDL unmarshals the arguments and invokes the method on the servant, then marshals the result back through the same path. Because both ends were generated from one language-neutral definition, the client and the servant may be in different languages and on different platforms, and neither has to know what the other is written in.

Compare the same exchange in message-oriented middleware. A publisher sends a message to a topic and immediately continues; it names no receiver and waits for nobody. The broker holds the message and forwards it to every subscriber interested in that topic, whether they were running when the message was published or connect later. Nothing in the publisher's code identifies a receiver, and nothing in a subscriber's code identifies a publisher — which is exactly the decoupling that a method call cannot offer.

Exam traps

  • Middleware's position is part of its definition: above the network and below the application software. Its two jobs are making the network transparent and hiding the platform details.
  • The three reasons heterogeneity happens — different solutions suit different parts, users choose their own vendors, legacy systems keep working — are asked for, and they are organisational as much as technical.
  • CORBA is a specification, not a product, and it is language-neutral and vendor-neutral. An answer that treats it as an implementation misses the point of the IDL.
  • Proxies are on the client side and skeletons on the server side, both generated from the IDL. The interface repository is what makes dynamic invocation possible, and GIOP and IIOP are the message definitions and their TCP/IP specialisation.
  • Java RMI's cost is single-language, and that is the whole comparison with CORBA. Presenting them as alternatives of equal reach contradicts the middleware purpose.
  • MQTT is publish-subscribe with a broker and topics, aimed at constrained devices and unreliable links, and its header size is quoted as part of why. AMQP is binary and supports both publish-subscribe and request-response with queues and exchanges.

Full-marks answer

  1. Explain heterogeneity with its three causes, then define middleware by its position and its two jobs.
  2. Introduce CORBA as the object request broker specification from the Object Management Group, language-neutral and vendor-neutral through its IDL.
  3. Give CORBA's machinery: proxies and skeletons generated from the IDL, the interface repository and dynamic invocation, GIOP and IIOP, and the service list.
  4. Give Java RMI as the language-specific counterpart, with local syntax for remote methods, type checking, the binder, and single-language as its cost.
  5. Name the message-oriented family — MQTT, AMQP, CoAP, XMPP — and explain what changes when the unit of interaction is a message rather than a call.
  6. Describe MQTT: publish-subscribe, the broker, the topic as the decoupling mechanism, the header overhead, and the IoT motivation.
  7. Describe AMQP: a binary application-layer protocol, publish-subscribe and request-response, queues and exchanges.
  8. Close by comparing the three families on what they assume about the client, the server and the moment of contact.
