5.1.html:
In one line

Cloud computing is seen from two sides at once: as infrastructure, ubiquitous access to shared pools of configurable system resources that can be rapidly provisioned with minimal management effort, and as a business, the delivery of computing services over the Internet charged by usage like a public utility.

The explanation

The two definitions name different things — the mechanism and the business model — and an answer that gives only one of them has answered half the question. Companies offering these services are cloud providers. The utility analogy is the defining attribute, and it is what separates cloud computing from ordinary hosting: a host rents a machine, while a cloud sells a metered slice of a shared pool.

The reasoning behind it is that information and data processing can be done more efficiently on large farms of computing and storage systems accessible via the Internet. Two earlier models supply the ideas that made it possible. Grid computing, from the national laboratories in the early 1990s, targets scientific computing, pooling resources from multiple locations for a common goal. Utility computing, from IT companies in 2005 and 2006, targets enterprise computing and charges for specific usage rather than a flat rate. Grid contributes the pooling of resources for one goal; utility contributes billing by usage instead of buying.

Five technologies made cloud computing what it is, and each contributes one property: distributed systems and their peripherals, virtualization, Web 2.0, service orientation and utility computing. Virtualization supplies the isolation and multiplexing, so a provider can sell slices of one machine. Web 2.0 supplies the browser-based interface, so a user needs nothing installed. Service orientation supplies the interface idea, and utility computing the pricing. The idea came in the 1950s and the result arrived in 2007 — a gap worth stating, because it shows that the technology was ready long before the commercial model was.

Three axes keep the models apart. The delivery or service models say what the provider supplies: software, platform or infrastructure as a service. The deployment models say who the cloud is for and where control sits: public, private, community, hybrid. The defining attributes say what makes it cloud rather than ordinary hosting: utility pricing, Internet access and elasticity. A fourth list names the resources a cloud is built from.

How it runs

Follow the two definitions through one purchase. A company needing a hundred machines for a month does not buy them and does not rent a hundred fixed machines: it asks a provider for a hundred machines, receives them in minutes, and is billed for what it used. Rapid provisioning with minimal management effort is the infrastructure definition, and the bill at the end of the month is the business one.

The provider can sell those hundred slices because virtualization multiplexes one physical machine into many, and because demand from different customers peaks at different times, so the same hardware serves all of them. That multiplexing is what makes the price per hour lower than the owner's own cost of ownership, and it is why the model could not exist before virtualization was practical.

The pool is presented through a browser, so nothing has to be installed to use it — the Web 2.0 contribution — and the interface the customer programs against is stable enough to build on, which is the service-orientation contribution. Remove any one of the five technologies and some part of the customer's experience breaks: no virtualization and there are no slices to sell, no Web interface and there is something to install, no utility pricing and it is hosting again.

Exam traps

  • Both definitions are needed, and they are distinct — the mechanism and the business model. Giving the utility analogy without the infrastructure definition, or the reverse, halves the marks.
  • Grid computing and utility computing are the two precursors, and each contributes one idea: pooling for a common goal, and billing by usage. Presenting them as two names for the same thing loses the point.
  • The five technologies are virtualization, Web 2.0, service orientation, utility computing and distributed systems, with the property each supplies.
  • The 1950s idea against the 2007 arrival is a specific pair of dates that questions quote; the gap is the interesting part of it.
  • The three axes — delivery models, deployment models, defining attributes — are three different questions about one system, and mixing them is the commonest way to lose structure marks.
  • Elasticity belongs to the defining attributes, not to the delivery models.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give both definitions and name what each one describes.
  2. State the utility analogy as the defining attribute, and what it separates cloud computing from.
  3. Give the reasoning — efficiency at farm scale — and the two precursors with their decades, their targets and their one contribution each.
  4. List the five technologies with the property each supplies.
  5. Give the timeline: the idea in the 1950s, the result in 2007.
  6. Close with the three axes and what each one classifies, placing the service models, the deployment models and the defining attributes on them.
points: The defining attribute, and what separates cloud computing from ordinary hosting.
From the national laboratories in the early 1990s, targeting scientific computing by pooling resources from multiple locations for a common goal.
From IT companies in 2005 and 2006, targeting enterprise computing and charging for specific usage rather than a flat rate.
Distributed systems and their peripherals, virtualization, Web 2.0, service orientation and utility computing.
The idea came in the 1950s and the result arrived in 2007.
Delivery or service models, deployment models, and the defining attributes of utility pricing, Internet access and elasticity.

5.2.html:
In one line

Cloud computing offers on-demand, scalable and elastic computing with resources metered and charged by use, from a shared pool managed by a provider — and its benefits and its challenges are the same properties seen from the customer's side and the provider's.

The explanation

The defining characteristics are a set, and each one is doing work. On demand: capacity is acquired when it is wanted. A shared pool of resources with resource management: many customers use one pool, and the management of it is the provider's job. Internet technology for scalable and elastic services: the delivery mechanism is the network, and the service grows or shrinks with demand. Metering, and cost-effectiveness from resource multiplexing passed on to users. Two of those words must be kept apart: scalability is the ability to handle growth, while elasticity is acquiring and releasing resources automatically in response to a variable workload. Elasticity is the cloud's distinguishing property, and it is the one to define first when both are asked for.

Two further characteristics are named. Data storage and management: data is held in the cloud, closer to where it is used, and appears to users in a location-independent manner; the storage strategy can increase reliability and security while lowering communication cost, which is location transparency applied to data. And management: maintenance and security are operated by the providers, who are more efficient at it through specialisation and centralisation. The objection to that is worth stating with it — relinquishing control becomes a security question rather than a technical convenience.

The benefits fall into four families. Sharing: CPU cycles, storage and bandwidth are shared, and peak demands from different users do not coincide, so multiplexing raises utilisation. Aggregation: resources can be aggregated for data-intensive work, and shared data facilitates collaboration. Cost: no capital investment in a private infrastructure, and payment as you go for computing actually used. Capability and user convenience: elasticity accommodates very large peak-to-average ratios, and virtualization lets users work in familiar environments instead of learning a provider's.

The challenges sit beside those advantages, one line each. Availability of service: what happens when the provider cannot deliver? Data confidentiality and auditability, described as a serious problem. Vendor lock-in: diversity of services, data organisation and user interfaces limits the user's mobility. A data transfer bottleneck, since many applications are data-intensive and moving the data costs time and money. Then performance unpredictability, resource management, and security for sensitive applications such as healthcare, where the data is regulated as well as valuable.

How it runs

A workload with a very uneven demand curve, run in the cloud. For most of the year the application needs a handful of servers; for a few weeks it needs many times that. Bought outright, the infrastructure is sized for the peak and idle for the rest — the peak-to-average ratio is paid for all year.

In the cloud the capacity is acquired when demand rises and released when it falls, and the billing follows the capacity rather than the calendar. The release is as important as the acquisition: a resource that is given back stops being paid for, which is elasticity rather than mere scalability. Growth that only adds cannot be cheap; growth that adds and removes can be.

The same flexibility is where the challenges live. If the provider's service is unavailable, the application is unavailable with it, and no amount of internal redundancy answers that. Data that has moved into the pool has left the organisation's own boundary, so confidentiality and auditability become questions the customer can no longer settle alone. And the interfaces, the data organisation and the tooling are the provider's, which is what makes leaving expensive.

Exam traps

  • Scalability against elasticity is the discrimination this topic is usually testing. Scalability handles growth; elasticity acquires and releases automatically against a variable workload, and it is the distinguishing property.
  • Metering is part of the definition of cloud computing, not an optional commercial detail; it is what connects multiplexing to the customer's bill.
  • The benefits are grouped in four families — sharing, cost, capability and user convenience, with aggregation alongside sharing. An unordered list scores less.
  • The data storage characteristic is location independence for data, and the management characteristic carries its own objection — control that is relinquished becomes a security question.
  • Vendor lock-in, data confidentiality and auditability, data transfer bottleneck, availability of service, performance unpredictability, resource management and security for sensitive applications are the named challenges.
  • The peak-to-average ratio is the argument for elasticity in one phrase, and it is worth writing into the answer.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the on-demand, scalable and elastic description with metered charging from a shared pool.
  2. Define scalability and elasticity separately, and say which one distinguishes the cloud.
  3. Give the two further characteristics — data storage and management — each with its qualification.
  4. List the benefits in four families: sharing and aggregation, cost, capability, user convenience.
  5. List the challenges with a clause each, keeping the ordered set.
  6. Close with the connection between the two lists: the flexibility that produces the benefits is the same property that produces the risks.
points: Acquiring and releasing resources automatically against a variable workload — the cloud's distinguishing property.
The ability to handle growth, which is a different property from elasticity.
Resources are metered and charged by use, which is what passes the benefit of resource multiplexing on to the customer.
Data held in the cloud, closer to where it is used, appearing to users in a location-independent manner.
Maintenance and security operated by the providers, who are more efficient through specialisation and centralisation.
Four families: sharing and aggregation, cost, capability, and user convenience.
Availability of service, data confidentiality and auditability, vendor lock-in, a data transfer bottleneck, performance unpredictability, resource management, and security for sensitive applications.

5.3.t: Cloud service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
5.3.html:
In one line

The three service models are a stack: Infrastructure as a Service gives compute resources, CPU, virtual machines and storage, Platform as a Service gives a platform on which to deploy applications using tools the provider supports, and Software as a Service gives applications supplied by the provider.

The explanation

The models are easiest to hold as a division of responsibility, because that is what each one actually sells. In IaaS the customer may run arbitrary software on the infrastructure, including its own operating system, and Amazon EC2 is the example. In PaaS the customer controls only the application: the platform, its runtime and its tools are the provider's. In SaaS the application itself is the provider's, and the customer simply uses it — Gmail and Salesforce are the two examples to name.

The stack ordering matters because each layer is built on the one below it and each one sells a different thing, which is why the lower layers are not completely transparent to the upper ones. It also explains who is responsible for what: as the stack is climbed, the customer's responsibility shrinks toward configuration and use, and the provider's grows toward running the machine.

A cloud service involves four families of activity, and they are the answer to "what does a provider actually operate?". Service management and provisioning: virtualization, provisioning, operations and systems management, quality-of-service management, billing, SLA management and backups. Security management: identity and authentication, intrusion prevention and detection, cryptography, physical security, access control, audit and trails, firewalls. Customer services: assistance and online help, subscriptions, business intelligence, reporting. Integration services: data management and development.

How it runs

Take one application and place it at each level. At the IaaS level the customer chooses the number of virtual machines, their operating systems, their storage and their networking, and installs everything above that itself. The provider runs the hardware, the virtualization and the physical security, and nothing else — which is why the customer may run arbitrary software here and why the operational burden stays with the customer.

At the PaaS level the machines and the runtime belong to the provider. The customer submits the application and its configuration, and the platform supplies the runtime, the scaling and much of the operational tooling. The customer controls only the application, in exchange for not caring which machine is running it or how many of them there are.

At the SaaS level the application itself is the service. The customer is a user, the interfaces are the provider's, and the data lives in the provider's storage. The same four families of activity are being run by the provider at all three levels — provisioning, security management, customer services and integration — but the share of them the customer still performs falls as the stack is climbed, and that fall is the whole content of the three models.

Exam traps

  • Each model is defined by who controls what: IaaS has the customer running arbitrary software including the operating system, PaaS gives control of the application only, SaaS gives the application itself.
  • The examples must be attached to the right layer: Amazon EC2 for IaaS, Gmail and Salesforce for SaaS. PaaS examples are named by vendors rather than by a single famous service.
  • The stack is ordered, and each layer sells a different thing, which is why lower layers are not wholly transparent upward. That sentence answers the "why a stack" question.
  • A cloud service's four families of activity — service management and provisioning, security management, customer services, integration services — are asked for as groupings. A flat list mixes layers of meaning.
  • Billing, SLA management and backups belong under service management and provisioning, not under customer services.
  • Identity and authentication, intrusion prevention and detection, cryptography and firewalls belong under security management, and the list is part of the answer rather than an aside.

Full-marks answer

  1. Name the three service models and state that they are a stack.
  2. Define each by the division of responsibility, with the example for IaaS and for SaaS.
  3. Explain the stack: each layer built on the one below, each selling a different thing, and the customer's responsibility falling as it is climbed.
  4. Give the four families of activity a cloud service involves, with the items under each.
  5. Place a single application at each of the three levels to show the same software under three different divisions of labour.
  6. Close on why the distinction matters commercially: the same workload costs and risks different things at different layers.
points: Each layer is built on the one below and sells a different thing, so lower layers are not completely transparent to the upper ones.
Virtualization, provisioning, operations and systems management, quality of service, billing, SLA management and backups.
Identity and authentication, intrusion prevention and detection, cryptography, physical security, access control, audit and trails, and firewalls.
Assistance and online help, subscriptions, business intelligence and reporting.

5.4.t: Cloud deployment models: Public, Private, Hybrid, Community
5.4.html:
In one line

A cloud deployment model is a specific configuration of environment parameters such as the accessibility and proprietorship of the infrastructure and the storage size, and the four models — public, private, hybrid and community — are separated not by hardware but by who controls the infrastructure and where it sits.

The explanation

Deployment models define the type of access to the cloud — how the cloud is located. The point that makes the four models one idea rather than four products is that the same physical data centre can be public for one customer and private for another: what differs is the arrangement, not the machines.

A public cloud is available to the general public or a large industry group and is owned by the organisation selling the services. A private cloud is operated solely for one organisation, with little technical difference from a public one; it is also called internal or corporate. A community cloud is shared by several organisations with shared concerns, and its difference from the private model is exactly the set of users. A hybrid cloud is two or more clouds bound by standardised technology that enables data and application portability.

Read down a column and the four models become four settings of a single trade: control against convenience. The public cloud is cheapest and easiest to set up, giving up security, control and reliability. The private cloud is the opposite in every one of those rows and the most expensive model. The hybrid buys the elastic part from a public cloud while keeping the sensitive part in-house. The community cloud shares the cost, and is the one row that is not high — its capacity is fixed.

Each model's advantages carry their own disadvantages and suit a particular use case. Public: hassle-free management, high scalability and reduced cost, at the price of reliability and data privacy, suited to fluctuating demand. Private: bespoke, flexible, secure and reliable, at considerable expense, suited to mission-critical operations that must stay under one company's control. Community: cost reduction, improved security and collaboration, at a higher cost than public and with fixed capacity, suited to joint projects between organisations. Hybrid: sensitive workloads stay private while the rest bursts to the public cloud.

Moving to the cloud has consequences beyond architecture, and they are grouped here as ethical issues. It relinquishes control to third-party services and stores data on multiple sites, and the implications are unauthorised access, data corruption, and infrastructure failure with service unavailability. De-perimeterisation is the removal of the boundary between an organisation and the outside world. Once systems and data cross that boundary, they have to be protected on multiple levels — using encryption, secure protocols, secure systems and data-level authentication — rather than by the network boundary that no longer separates anything. The conclusion to state is that once the perimeter is gone, identity and access management and data-level security are the only controls left.

How it runs

One organisation, two workloads, one deployment decision. The first workload is a public-facing web application with spiky traffic and nothing sensitive in it: a public cloud gives the elasticity and the low entry cost, and none of the things given up are needed.

The second is a regulated data store that must stay under the organisation's own control. The same public cloud cannot host it, so it runs on a private cloud: dedicated resources, higher cost, and the security and reliability properties the workload's regulation demands. Neither choice is wrong; they are two settings of the control-against-convenience trade, applied to two different workloads.

A hybrid binds them. The sensitive store stays private and the web front end bursts into the public cloud, and what makes the combination work is standardised technology that lets data and applications move between the two without being rewritten — portability is the requirement, not merely the intention. Whichever arrangement is chosen, the data now crosses an organisation's boundary, and the controls that remain are identity, access management and data-level protection rather than a firewall at the edge.

Exam traps

  • A deployment model is defined by accessibility and proprietorship, and the four models are separated by who controls the infrastructure. "Where the servers are" is not the discriminator.
  • The private cloud has little technical difference from a public one; what differs is operation and ownership. Saying it uses different technology contradicts the topic.
  • The community cloud differs from the private one by its set of users, which is exactly the sentence examiners look for.
  • The hybrid is defined by standardised technology enabling data and application portability — two or more clouds alone is not yet a hybrid.
  • Each model's use case has to be attached: fluctuating demand for public, mission-critical work under one company's control for private, joint projects for community.
  • De-perimeterisation is the removal of the boundary, and the answer should end with the controls that survive it — encryption, secure protocols, secure systems, data-level authentication, identity and access management.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define a deployment model by accessibility and proprietorship, and state the four models.
  2. Define each of the four with its ownership and its users, and say what community differs from private by.
  3. Give the trade each one sets: public cheapest and least controlled, private the opposite and most expensive, hybrid elastic in parts, community shared with fixed capacity.
  4. Give the advantages, disadvantages and use case of each model in turn.
  5. Explain the consequences of moving to the cloud: loss of control, data on multiple sites, unauthorised access, corruption, unavailability.
  6. Define de-perimeterisation and close with the layered controls that replace the network boundary, ending on identity and access management as what remains.
points: Available to the general public or a large industry group, owned by the organisation selling the services.
Operated solely for one organisation, with little technical difference from a public one.
Shared by several organisations with shared concerns; it differs from the private model by its set of users.
Two or more clouds bound by standardised technology that enables data and application portability.
Public is cheapest and gives up security, control and reliability; private is the opposite and the most expensive; hybrid keeps the sensitive part in-house.
The removal of the boundary between an organisation and the outside world, after which identity and access management and data-level security are the controls that remain.

6.1.t: Basics of virtualization: Hypervisors (Type I & II)
6.1.html:
In one line

Virtualization is the process by which one computer hosts the appearance of many computers — running multiple operating systems on a single physical system, sharing the underlying hardware — and the hypervisor is the software that makes it possible.

The explanation

Virtualization is the foundation of cloud computing because it turns physical resources into a pool from which virtual resources are allocated, improving IT throughput and reducing costs. A virtual machine is an isolated runtime environment comprising a guest operating system and its applications, and the stack is a physical machine, a virtualization platform such as Xen, KVM or VMware, and the virtual systems above it.

Six kinds of virtualization are named, and each is virtualization applied to a different layer. Application: the application is stored and run from a server rather than on the local machine. Network: several virtual networks, each with its own separate control and data plane, coexist on one physical network. Desktop: the desktop and its applications are separated from the physical client device. Storage: physical storage is aggregated into a pool that appears as a single device. Server: one physical server becomes several isolated virtual servers, each with its own operating system. Data: many sources are presented as one view.

A hypervisor, also called a virtual machine manager, lets multiple operating systems share one hardware host. Each guest appears to have the host's processor, memory and other resources to itself. The hypervisor controls the host processor and resources, allocating what is needed to each system in turn, and it makes sure the guest operating systems cannot disrupt each other. It sits directly between the physical hardware and its operating system, supports hardware-level virtualization, and provides hypercalls to its guests.

The two types differ by one layer. Type I runs directly on the host and is also called native or bare-metal; it has direct access to hardware and is used in servers and data centres, with Xen and KVM as examples. Type II runs as an application in a host system and is also called hosted; it reaches the hardware through the host operating system and is used on desktops, with VMware Workstation as the example. The consequence to state is that in the Type II case a guest's input and output passes through two operating systems.

A hypervisor has five responsibilities, one per virtualized resource: isolating and emulating resources in general, scheduling virtual machines on the CPU, managing memory, emulating I/O devices — which an unmodified operating system looks for and will not boot without — and networking, along with managing the virtual machines themselves.

CPU virtualization rests on the fact that a virtual machine is a duplicate of a computer system and most of its instructions execute on the host processor in native mode. The rest are privileged instructions, which trap when executed outside privileged mode. Among them, control-sensitive instructions change the configuration of resources, and behaviour-sensitive ones behave differently depending on configuration. An architecture is virtualizable when those instructions are trapped in the virtual machine monitor, which mediates hardware access from different virtual machines. RISC architectures virtualize naturally, while x86 required binary translation, paravirtualization or hardware-assisted extensions.

Memory virtualization shares the system's RAM, allocating it dynamically to the virtual machines. Traditionally the mapping from virtual to machine memory takes one stage through page tables. Virtualized, it takes two: the guest operating system maps virtual addresses to its own physical memory, and the virtual machine monitor maps those to real machine memory. The second stage exists so that a guest cannot name memory belonging to another guest or to the hypervisor. The price is an extra translation on every access, which nested page tables recover.

I/O virtualization has three approaches, each trading compatibility against overhead. Full device emulation replicates device enumeration, identification, interrupts and DMA in software in the virtual machine monitor, so unmodified guests work at a very high overhead. Direct I/O gives a virtual machine direct access to devices, achieving close-to-native performance, although a device reclaimed from one machine may be left in an arbitrary state. Hardware-assisted virtualization puts the remapping and isolation in hardware, because software emulation costs too much; a virtual device remaps the guest's and the real I/O addresses and multiplexes the physical device.

Xen is the open-source hypervisor developed by Cambridge University, and its architecture is a micro-kernel hypervisor that separates policy from mechanism, leaving policy to Domain 0. It includes no device drivers natively, only a mechanism by which a guest operating system reaches the physical devices. The guest operating system with control ability is Domain 0 and the others are Domain U, and Domain 0 is loaded first at boot to allocate and map hardware resources for the guest domains.

The benefits are five, and each is a cloud property restated at the machine level. Sharing of resources: the multiplexing that makes pay-per-usage economical. Isolation: virtual machines are isolated from each other as if physically separated, which is what makes multi-tenancy possible. Encapsulation: a virtual machine encapsulates a complete computing environment, so a whole machine becomes one file. Hardware independence: virtual machines run independently of the underlying hardware. Portability: they can be migrated between different hosts, which is what live migration is.

The vulnerability is the flip side of the position: because the hypervisor sits between every guest and the hardware, it is a single point of attack that can see every guest. The threat is malicious software running on the same server, attacking the hypervisor and reaching other virtual machines through it — the term for that is VM escape. NoHype is one research answer: remove the hypervisor, and there is nothing to attack, while still retaining the needs of a virtualized cloud infrastructure. The trade-off to close on is that the isolation the hypervisor provides is also the isolation it must be trusted to provide.

How it runs

A guest instruction, followed through the layers. Most instructions from the guest execute on the host processor in native mode, which is why a virtual machine performs close to a physical one for ordinary work.

An instruction that would touch a privileged resource does not execute: it traps into the virtual machine monitor, which inspects it and performs the operation on the guest's behalf, keeping the effect inside the guest's own slice of memory and devices. A guest's attempt to reach a page belonging to another guest therefore fails in the second translation stage rather than in the guest's own page tables, which is the mechanism that keeps one tenant out of another's data.

I/O is where the cost shows. Under full device emulation, every device access is replicated in software and the guest never touches the hardware, so an unmodified operating system runs at a very high overhead. Under direct access, the device is handed to the guest and performance approaches native, at the price of the hypervisor having to reclaim and reset a device that a guest may have left in any state. Hardware assistance is the middle answer: the remapping and isolation happen in silicon, so neither the software emulation cost nor the unrestricted device access is paid.

Exam traps

  • The six kinds of virtualization are application, network, desktop, storage, server and data. Each is virtualization of a different layer, and naming them without the layer earns little.
  • Type I runs directly on the host, Type II runs as an application in a host system. The named consequence is that a guest's I/O passes through two operating systems under Type II.
  • Control-sensitive and behaviour-sensitive instructions are the two classes that matter for virtualizability, and RISC against x86 is the standard example of an architecture that virtualizes naturally against one that needed help.
  • Memory virtualization takes two mapping stages, and the second exists for isolation — a guest must not be able to name another guest's memory. Nested page tables recover the extra translation cost.
  • Xen's three defining facts are the micro-kernel design, the separation of policy from mechanism, and Domain 0 loaded first with the guests as Domain U.
  • The hypervisor is a single point of attack that can see every guest, VM escape is the threat, and NoHype removes the hypervisor instead of hardening it. The trade-off sentence is the conclusion, not an optional extra.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define virtualization and the virtual machine, and state why it is the foundation of cloud computing.
  2. List the six kinds with the layer each applies to.
  3. Define the hypervisor and give its responsibilities: isolation and emulation, CPU scheduling, memory, I/O, networking and virtual machine management.
  4. Compare Type I and Type II by where they run, what they can reach, where each is used, and the double operating-system path in Type II.
  5. Explain CPU virtualization through privileged, control-sensitive and behaviour-sensitive instructions, virtualizability, and why RISC and x86 differ.
  6. Explain memory virtualization's two-stage mapping, its isolation purpose and its cost.
  7. Compare the three I/O approaches on compatibility against overhead.
  8. Describe Xen's architecture, give the five benefits, and close with the vulnerability, VM escape and NoHype.
points: An isolated runtime environment comprising a guest operating system and its applications.
Application, network, desktop, storage, server and data virtualization.
Also called a virtual machine manager: it lets multiple operating systems share one hardware host and keeps them from disrupting each other.
Also called native or bare-metal: it runs directly on the host with direct access to hardware, and is used in servers and data centres.
Also called hosted: it runs as an application in a host system, so a guest's input and output passes through two operating systems.
Most instructions run natively; privileged instructions trap, and the control-sensitive and behaviour-sensitive ones decide whether an architecture is virtualizable.
Two mapping stages, so that a guest cannot name memory belonging to another guest or to the hypervisor.
Full device emulation, direct I/O, or hardware-assisted remapping and isolation.
An open-source micro-kernel hypervisor that separates policy from mechanism, leaving policy to Domain 0.
Virtual machines are isolated from each other as if physically separated, which is what makes multi-tenancy possible.
Malicious software on the same server attacking the hypervisor in order to reach other virtual machines.

6.2.html:
In one line

Both virtualize, at different levels: a virtual machine virtualizes the machine, with the hypervisor replicating hardware in software, while a container virtualizes the operating system, giving isolated environments within the same host kernel.

The explanation

A virtual machine is a software program that emulates the functionality of physical hardware or a computing system. It runs on top of the hypervisor, which replicates the underlying hardware resources in software. The physical hardware is the host machine and the virtual machine running on it is the guest machine. The virtual machine contains what it needs to run its applications — storage, memory and networking — and a guest usually runs a complete operating system of its own, which is why a virtual machine image is measured in gigabytes.

Containerization creates abstraction at an operating-system level, letting several isolated workloads share the same physical resources. A container is a unit of software that is lightweight but still bundles the code, its dependencies and the configuration into a single image. Containers can run on bare-metal servers, on hypervisors, or in cloud infrastructure. The defining difference is the sentence to keep: a containerization engine creates isolated environments within the same host system kernel, separate only in their binaries and libraries — and that is what makes them more resource-efficient compared with virtual machines.

The comparison itself has four rows. A virtual machine's abstraction is at the hardware level, while a container's is at the operating-system level, so a container sees a user space. A virtual machine instance includes a full guest operating system, while a container image includes only the code, dependencies and configuration. Containers are more resource-efficient and faster to start. Containers are less secure, because the underlying operating system is shared. Two consequences follow: virtual machines can run different guest operating systems, whereas all containers on a host run atop the same kernel; and the shared kernel is exactly the surface that makes the security difference real rather than theoretical.

How it runs

Take one application and run it both ways. As a virtual machine, it is packaged with a complete guest operating system, and the hypervisor gives that operating system virtual hardware. Booting means booting a kernel, which is why the image is measured in gigabytes and why startup takes seconds. Nothing of the guest's kernel is shared with the host or with any other guest, so two virtual machines on the same hardware may run entirely different operating systems.

As a container, the application is packaged with its dependencies and configuration but with no kernel at all. The containerization engine starts a process on the host's existing kernel and gives it an isolated view of the filesystem, the process space and the network, so startup is the time it takes to start a process rather than to boot a system — which is what allows far more of them on the same hardware.

Now consider the cost of that efficiency. Because every container on a host shares one kernel, a flaw that lets a process escape its isolation reaches the host and therefore every other container on it. A virtual machine pays for its extra layer of operating system in memory and startup time, and receives in exchange a boundary that is enforced below the level at which any guest code runs. That exchange — resources and speed against the strength of the separation — is the whole comparison, and it is why both are still used.

Exam traps

  • The one-line discrimination is the level of abstraction: a virtual machine virtualizes the machine, a container virtualizes the operating system.
  • The reason containers are lighter is that they share the host kernel and contain no guest operating system. Efficiency is the effect; the shared kernel is the cause.
  • The security difference is the price of that sharing. Containers are less secure because the underlying operating system is shared, not because their tooling is newer.
  • Host machine and guest machine are the two terms for the physical hardware and the virtual machine running on it, and both are asked for by name.
  • A container image holds the code, its dependencies and the configuration. Saying it holds "the application" leaves out what makes it reproducible.
  • Containers can run on bare metal, on hypervisors or in cloud infrastructure — they are not tied to a host operating system's own deployment.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define the virtual machine, name the hypervisor as what it runs on, and define host and guest.
  2. Say what a virtual machine contains, and use the image size as evidence that a guest operating system is inside it.
  3. Define containerization as abstraction at the operating-system level, and the container as a lightweight unit bundling code, dependencies and configuration.
  4. State where containers can run, then give the defining difference: one engine, one host kernel, isolation in binaries and libraries.
  5. Give the comparison row by row: level of abstraction, what the image contains, resource efficiency and startup speed, and security.
  6. Close with the two consequences — different guest operating systems against one shared kernel — and the trade between them.
points: A software program that emulates the functionality of physical hardware or a computing system, running on the hypervisor.
The physical hardware on which the hypervisor runs and the virtual machines are guests.
A lightweight unit of software that bundles the code, its dependencies and the configuration into a single image.
Abstraction at an operating-system level, with isolated environments inside the same host system kernel.
Containers share the host kernel and contain no guest operating system, so they are lighter and faster to start.
Sharing the underlying operating system makes containers less secure than virtual machines, whose boundary the hypervisor enforces.

6.3.html:
In one line

The cloud reference architecture draws the provider in layers — service, resource abstraction and control, and physical resource, with cloud service management beside them — and names six actors: consumer, provider, auditor, broker, developer and carrier.

The explanation

The provider's four layers are what has to be drawn. The service layer holds the three delivery models as the customer sees them: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS. The resource abstraction and control layer holds the hypervisors, virtual machines and control software — this is where virtualization lives. The physical resource layer holds hardware and facility: servers, storage, network, power, cooling and physical security. Beside the three sits cloud service management: business support, provisioning and configuration, and portability and interoperability. Running vertically through all of them are security, privacy and performance, which is what makes them cross-cutting rather than a fifth layer.

The NIST reference model's six actors each answer a different question about the same service. The consumer is the principal stakeholder that maintains a business relationship with the provider — the party whose workload it is. The provider is the entity that makes services available. The auditor conducts an audit to express an opinion, verifying conformance to standards, and SLA verification depends on it — which is the actor most often forgotten, and the one that connects this topic to the agreements that govern the service. The broker manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates between providers and consumers, through intermediation, aggregation and arbitrage. The developer builds applications on the provider's platform, and the carrier provides the connectivity.

How it runs

Take one service request and hand it round the actors. A consumer has a workload and a business relationship with a provider; it asks for capacity, and the provider allocates it out of the physical resource layer, through the abstraction and control layer where the hypervisors live, and delivers it as one of the service models at the service layer.

If the consumer does not buy directly, the broker is in between: it negotiates, may aggregate services from several providers, and may take advantage of price differences between them. The developer is the party who writes what runs on the platform, and the carrier is the network that makes any of it reachable. When the consumer wants evidence that the service meets its commitments, the auditor provides it by checking conformance to standards rather than by taking the provider's word.

Through every one of those steps run the three vertical concerns. Security governs who may do what at each layer, privacy governs what data may be where, and performance governs whether the promise is met — which is why they are drawn as columns rather than as a layer, and why the same guarantee has to be examined separately at the service, the control and the physical levels.

Exam traps

  • The provider's three stacked layers are service, resource abstraction and control, and physical resource, with cloud service management beside them and security, privacy and performance running vertically through all three.
  • Virtualization belongs in the resource abstraction and control layer; the three delivery models belong at the service layer. Placing either in the other layer is a common slip.
  • The auditor is the actor that verifies conformance to standards, and SLA verification depends on it. An answer that lists five actors has usually dropped this one.
  • The broker's three activities are intermediation, aggregation and arbitrage, and they are named in the model.
  • Cloud service management contains business support, provisioning and configuration, and portability and interoperability — it is a support column, not a delivery layer.
  • Each actor is defined by its relationship to the service, so the answer should give the relationship rather than a job title alone.

Full-marks answer

  1. Draw the provider's layers in order from the customer's view down: service, resource abstraction and control, physical resource.
  2. Say what sits in each layer, ending with hypervisors and control software in the middle one.
  3. Add cloud service management beside the stack, with its three contents.
  4. Add security, privacy and performance as vertical concerns that cross every layer.
  5. Name the six actors of the NIST reference model and give the relationship each one has to the service.

6.4.html:
In one line

Provisioning is the decision of how much capacity to commit to a customer, and it is a commercial optimum rather than a technical one: underprovision and the service level agreement breaks, overprovision and the resources are paid for and unused.

The explanation

Providers supply cloud services by signing SLAs with end users, committing enough CPU, memory and bandwidth for a preset period. Underprovisioning leads to broken agreements and penalties. Overprovisioning leads to resource underutilisation and a decrease in revenue. Five sources of difficulty make the estimate hard: unpredictable consumer demand, software and hardware failures, the heterogeneity of services, power management, and conflicts between the agreements already signed.

Efficient virtual machine provisioning depends on the cloud architecture and on how the cloud infrastructure is managed. In a virtualised cluster it demands three capabilities: efficient installation of virtual machines, live migration of virtual machines, and fast recovery from failures. Users treat virtual machines as physical hosts with customised operating systems for their own applications, which is why the ability to install and move them quickly is the provider's whole product. Amazon EC2 uses Xen as the virtual machine monitor — the same monitor as IBM's Blue Cloud — and provides predefined virtual machine templates. IBM's Blue Cloud provides no templates, and Microsoft applies virtualization in Azure.

Three provisioning methods answer demand differently, and each has its failure mode. Demand-driven provisioning adds or removes instances by utilisation: below a threshold capacity is decreased, above it capacity is increased. It is easy to implement, and it fails when the workload changes abruptly, because by the time the threshold has been crossed the capacity is already needed. Event-driven provisioning anticipates a specific time event, such as a holiday period, and works well if the event is predicted correctly. Popularity-driven provisioning creates instances for the applications that are currently popular, with the same risk of wasted resources if the expected traffic does not arrive.

Two closing ideas complete the unit. The software stack of a cloud is built from scratch for rigorous goals, so every layer is designed for high throughput, high availability and fault tolerance; and the lower layers are not completely transparent to the upper layers, because each layer sells a different thing. Runtime support services are the operational pair that keeps a cluster running: cluster monitoring collects the runtime status of the whole cluster, and a scheduler queues tasks and assigns them to nodes by availability. The distributed scheduler has special characteristics, such as being able to schedule programs written in the MapReduce style.

A short list of cloud service tasks and trends closes the topic: SaaS is the top layer for business applications, and customer relationship management offered the first successful SaaS on the cloud; SaaS tools also serve distributed collaboration, financial and human-resources management. PaaS is provided by Google, Salesforce.com and Facebook among others, and IaaS by Amazon, Windows Azure and Rackspace. Collocation services require multiple providers to work together to support supply chains in manufacturing, and network cloud services provide communications from carriers.

How it runs

A provider signing an agreement and then living with it. The provider commits CPU, memory and bandwidth for a preset period at a price. If demand exceeds the commitment, the agreement breaks and penalties follow; if demand falls short, the capacity is still there and the revenue per unit of hardware falls. Neither error is recoverable by engineering alone, which is why the estimate is described as a commercial optimum.

The demand-driven method, in operation. Utilisation is watched against two thresholds. When it rises past the upper one, capacity is added; when it falls below the lower one, capacity is removed. For a smooth workload this tracks demand closely at almost no cost. For an abrupt change it is too late by construction: the threshold is crossed only after the new load has arrived, and capacity that takes minutes to start is needed in the first seconds.

Event-driven provisioning goes the other way and commits in advance. Capacity is planned for a known occasion, and if the prediction is right the provider is ready before the traffic arrives. Popularity-driven provisioning does something similar for applications rather than dates, creating instances for whatever is currently popular. Both buy readiness with the risk of having paid for resources nobody uses — the same trade that underlies the whole provisioning problem, taken one step earlier in time.

Exam traps

  • The two errors are named and must be balanced in the answer: underprovisioning breaks the agreement, overprovisioning wastes resources and reduces revenue.
  • The five sources of difficulty — unpredictable demand, hardware and software failures, heterogeneity of services, power management, conflicting agreements — are asked for as a set.
  • The three capabilities of efficient provisioning in a virtualised cluster are efficient installation, live migration and fast recovery from failures.
  • Demand-driven provisioning's weakness is structural: by the time the threshold is crossed, the capacity is needed. It is not merely "slow".
  • Event-driven and popularity-driven both predict, and both pay for readiness with the risk of unused resources.
  • Cluster monitoring and the scheduler are the runtime support services, and the scheduler's special characteristic is scheduling MapReduce-style programs.

Full-marks answer

  1. State the provisioning problem as a commercial optimum, and give the two errors it balances.
  2. Give the five sources of difficulty in estimating demand.
  3. Give the three capabilities efficient virtual machine provisioning needs, and name the monitor and templates the named platforms use.
  4. Describe the three provisioning methods — demand-driven, event-driven, popularity-driven — with the mechanism and the failure mode of each.
  5. Describe the software stack's design goals and the fact that layers are not fully transparent to each other.
  6. Give the runtime support services, cluster monitoring and the scheduler, with the special scheduling characteristic.
  7. Close with the current service landscape: what SaaS serves, who provides PaaS and IaaS, and what collocation and network cloud services are.

7.1.t: Overview of AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
7.1.html:
In one line

A cloud platform is the whole of what a cloud provider offers — the three delivery models in one catalogue — and any platform is answered by three questions: what is rented, where it is, and how it is billed.

The explanation

A cloud provider is a company offering computing services over the Internet and charging for them by usage. The named providers map onto the delivery models: infrastructure as a service comes from Amazon, Windows Azure and Rackspace; platform as a service from Google, Salesforce.com and Facebook. The examples to attach are EC2 for infrastructure, Google App Engine and Windows Azure for platform, and Gmail and Salesforce for software.

AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the three platforms, and each has an origin to hold. AWS is the first mover with the largest catalogue; EC2 uses Xen as its virtual machine monitor, S3 is object storage and Lambda is serverless. Azure began as a managed application platform and then expanded into virtual machines and software as a service. Google Cloud began with App Engine and expanded into virtual machines and Kubernetes. Each now offers virtual machines, containers, functions and object storage, so choosing between them comes down to geography, price and ecosystem rather than to capability.

The services of a platform are best listed by layer. Compute: virtual central processing units and virtual main memory for the machines provisioned to end users. Storage: the provider supplies back-end storage for storing files. Network: network as a service provides routers, switches and bridges for the virtual machines. Load balancers: load balancing capability at the infrastructure layer. The providers named alongside these categories include Amazon Web Services, Rackspace, Netmagic Solutions, Tata Communications, Sify Technologies and Reliance.

The customer's view has advantages and disadvantages that mirror each other. The advantages: shared infrastructure, web access to the resources, a pay-as-per-use model, focus on the core business, and on-demand scalability. The disadvantages: security, since most providers cannot give complete security; maintenance and upgrade, because providers maintain the software but do not upgrade it for some organisations; and interoperability, because migrating a virtual machine from one provider to another is difficult, which leaves the customer facing vendor lock-in.

The pizza analogy makes the three delivery models concrete, and it is worth reproducing because it fixes the division of labour in one image. On premises is dining in at home: the customer manages everything. Infrastructure as a service is take and bake: the vendor supplies the dough, sauce, toppings and cheese, while the customer supplies the table, the oven and the fire. Platform as a service is pizza delivered: the vendor brings the finished pizza, and the customer provides the table and the drinks and manages only the application. Software as a service is dining out: everything is the restaurant's, and the customer manages only its data and its account.

Beyond the three models sits the wider family, XaaS — anything as a service — which delivers anything over a network rather than locally. HaaS, hardware as a service: managed service providers own the hardware and install it at customers' sites on demand. CaaS, communications as a service: telephony, instant messaging and video conferencing hosted in the vendor's cloud. DaaS, desktop as a service: desktops delivered as virtual services, with the provider backing up the data. SECaaS: outsourced security management covering anti-virus, encryption and authentication. DBaaS: a database platform through the cloud. TaaS: transport applications paid for by distance.

How it runs

One platform, one workload, seen from the customer's side. The customer signs up, gets a console, an API, a command-line interface and software development kits, and chooses a region and an availability zone inside it. Nothing about the physical hardware is chosen or known; what is chosen is where the workload is allowed to run.

The workload is then assembled from the platform's catalogue: a virtual machine from the compute layer, a volume or an object store from the storage layer, a virtual network with firewall rules, and a load balancer in front. Each of those is an API call, which is why the same three platforms converge — a widely used interface becomes the one everyone implements.

The bill follows the same shape. Compute is charged while the machine is running, storage while the bytes are held, and network traffic as it moves, which is why an idle platform costs almost nothing and a busy one costs in proportion to what it used. And the exit is deliberately not symmetrical: the concepts transfer between platforms, but the management interfaces, the identity model and the proprietary services do not — which is what the disadvantage list calls vendor lock-in.

Exam traps

  • The three platforms are AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, and each has its origin and its flagship service. Naming the providers without their origins is a thin answer.
  • The category lists are asked for by layer — compute, storage, network, load balancers — with the named providers alongside them.
  • The disadvantage list is specific: security, maintenance and upgrade, and interoperability leading to vendor lock-in. It is not a general complaint about the cloud.
  • The pizza analogy is examined as a mapping of responsibilities, so each model needs what the vendor supplies and what the customer still manages.
  • XaaS stands for anything as a service, and each family in it is defined by what is delivered over the network. Getting the acronyms and their meanings right is most of the marks.
  • Convergence and lock-in are two halves of one point: the services are APIs, so interfaces converge, and the proprietary parts are what hold a customer in place.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define a cloud platform and cloud provider, and give the three questions asked of any platform.
  2. Name the three platforms with the origin and flagship service of each, and state what choosing between them now comes down to.
  3. List the platform's services by layer, with the providers named for each category.
  4. Give the customer's advantages and disadvantages, ending on vendor lock-in through interoperability.
  5. Use the pizza analogy for the three delivery models, giving what the vendor supplies and what remains with the customer at each level.
  6. Close with XaaS and its families — HaaS, CaaS, DaaS, SECaaS, DBaaS, TaaS — defining each by what it delivers.

7.2.html:
In one line

Cloud storage comes in three shapes — object, block and file — and S3 and Blob are both object storage: objects in a flat namespace, each addressed by a key, used through an HTTP API.

The explanation

The three shapes are told apart by what the customer gets. Object storage holds objects in a flat namespace, each addressed by a key, and is used through an HTTP API — put an object, get an object. Block storage gives volumes of raw blocks attached to a virtual machine, which the guest operating system formats with a file system of its own. File storage gives files in directories, mounted as a shared directory by several instances at once. The three platforms each offer one of each, and the mapping is worth learning as a set: AWS has S3, EBS and EFS; Azure has Blob Storage, Managed Disks and Azure Files; Google has Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk and Filestore.

Two facts hold for both S3 and Blob, and they are the ones that explain how object storage behaves. A bucket or container is the top-level namespace and the unit of policy, region and naming. An object is addressed by its key within its bucket, and there are no real directories — what looks like a folder path is part of the key. The API is HTTP verbs on a URL — PUT, GET and DELETE — so the storage interface is REST, and anything that can make an HTTP request can use it.

Three further properties follow. Durability comes from replication and is separate from availability: a service can be designed for durability measured in a long run of nines while its availability in any given month is a smaller figure, because durability is about the object still existing while availability is about the service answering now. Access tiers trade retrieval cost against storage cost, so an object that is rarely read can be held cheaply and paid for when it is read. Lifecycle rules move objects between those tiers automatically as they age, which is what keeps a large store affordable without anyone remembering to change anything.

Database as a service then runs on top of the storage layer, and the distinction that matters is who administers the database. On a rented virtual machine it is infrastructure as a service with the customer's own database management system on top: the customer sizes it, patches it, backs it up and runs its replicas. A managed database keeps the platform and removes the administration — provisioning, maintenance, replication, indexing and tuning are the provider's. The two families are relational, with SQL, schemas, transactions and joins, and non-relational, which covers key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores. The named examples in this course are both non-relational.

How it runs

Put an object and read it back. The client makes an HTTP request naming the bucket, the key and the object's bytes, and the service stores it and answers with an identifier. Nothing was mounted and no file system was created: the key is the whole address, and the bucket is the whole namespace, so the second write of the same key replaces the first rather than making a second version alongside it.

Read it back and the replication is invisible. The request goes to the service, which serves the object from whichever replica is convenient, and because durability is a property of the replication rather than of any one disk, no single machine's failure changes the answer. The availability figure and the durability figure are different numbers measured against different questions, which is why the design can promise so much more on the second.

Now age the object. A lifecycle rule moves it from a frequently-read tier to one that is cheaper to hold and dearer to read, and nothing about the object's address or the code that reads it changes. The cost curve of the store bends without the application being touched — which is the practical reason object storage is where large datasets live.

Exam traps

  • The three shapes are object, block and file, and each is defined by what the customer is given: objects with keys, raw blocks to format, files in directories to mount.
  • The mapping of the three platforms onto the three shapes is asked for as a set: S3, EBS and EFS; Blob, Managed Disks and Azure Files; Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk and Filestore.
  • A bucket is the unit of policy, region and naming, and an object is addressed by key. There are no real directories, which is the point most often missed.
  • Durability and availability are separate properties with separate figures. Presenting them as one number loses the distinction the topic exists to make.
  • Access tiers and lifecycle rules work together: tiers change the cost of holding and reading, rules move objects between them automatically.
  • Database as a service is distinguished by who administers the database. Relational against non-relational is the second axis, with key-value, document, wide-column and graph as the non-relational families.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the three shapes of cloud storage with what each one provides.
  2. Map each of the three platforms onto the three shapes.
  3. Explain the bucket as the top-level namespace and the object as key-addressed within it, with no real directories.
  4. Describe the API as HTTP verbs on a URL, making the storage interface REST.
  5. State the durability against availability distinction, then access tiers and lifecycle rules as the cost mechanism.
  6. Introduce database as a service, contrast it with running a database on a rented machine, and give the two families with their examples.

7.3.html:
In one line

Cloud compute comes in three shapes — virtual machines, containers and serverless functions — differing in how much of the stack the customer manages, and each step down the ladder removes a layer the customer patches, scales and pays for.

The explanation

The three shapes are best held as a division of labour. Virtual machines: EC2, Azure Virtual Machines and Compute Engine, where the customer manages the guest operating system, the patches, the runtime and the scaling. Containers: ECS, AKS and GKE, where the customer manages the image and the orchestration, and the orchestrator schedules it. Serverless functions: Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Functions, where the customer manages only the code, which is started by an event and billed per invocation.

EC2 is a web service providing elastic computing power, letting customers create and manage virtual machines. It uses Xen as its virtual machine monitor, the same monitor as IBM's Blue Cloud, and provides predefined virtual machine templates. Four terms belong to it: an instance is one running virtual machine; an instance type is its CPU, memory and network profile; an AMI is the template an instance is launched from; and a security group is the set of firewall rules around an instance. Purchasing comes in three forms — on demand, reserved and spot — which are respectively billing per second, a commitment for a discount, and reclaimable spare capacity. Auto-scaling is demand-driven provisioning implemented as a service.

Serverless means the provider runs the code and the customer manages no servers. An event starts the code and it ends when the function returns, so nothing is billed while it is not running; billing is per invocation and per execution duration. Scaling is per request and automatic, because the platform runs as many copies as the traffic needs, which is elasticity pushed to its limit and measured in invocations rather than machines. Functions are stateless between invocations, so any state belongs in storage or a database rather than in the function itself. The trade, taken one step further than containers: there is no operating system to configure, execution time is capped, and a cold start can add latency to the first request.

Google Compute Engine is the counterpart of EC2 and Azure Virtual Machines: instances launched from images, persistent disks attached to them, a virtual network with firewall rules, and load balancing. Its distinguishing feature is the ecosystem around it — its Kubernetes origins and the data and machine-learning services on top. All three platforms converge, and the reason is stated in one line: the services are APIs, and a widely used API becomes a de facto standard. That makes lock-in partial rather than total: the concepts transfer between platforms, but the management APIs, the identity model and the proprietary services do not.

Using a platform at all runs through a console, an API, a command-line interface and software development kits. It is organised by region, a geographic area, and availability zone, an isolated set of data centres within that region. That is a fault-domain rule as much as a naming convention: replicas are placed across zones so that the failure of one zone is survivable, and the price of the placement is that data crossing between zones costs more than data staying inside one. The provider's own requirements are the reference architecture — orchestration, resource abstraction and control, physical resources, and management — and its software stack is designed for high throughput, high availability and fault tolerance, with each layer providing an interface to the one above it.

How it runs

The same function, placed at each rung of the ladder. On a virtual machine the customer launches an instance from a template, attaches storage, opens the ports in a security group, installs the runtime and the code, and is then responsible for patching the operating system and for scaling by starting more instances.

In a container the runtime and the code arrive as one image, and the orchestrator decides where it runs and keeps the number of copies at the declared value. The customer still owns the image and the orchestration, but the machine underneath is no longer theirs to patch. With a serverless function there is nothing underneath at all: the code is uploaded, an event triggers it, the platform runs as many copies as the traffic needs, and the bill counts invocations and milliseconds of execution rather than machines.

Then measure the same workload on all three. A steady high load is cheapest on a reserved virtual machine, because a machine paid for by the month is cheaper per unit of work than one billed per invocation. A spiky or rare load is cheapest on functions, because the idle time is free. Containers sit between the two, which is why all three shapes survive on the same platform rather than one replacing the others.

Exam traps

  • The three shapes are compared by what the customer manages, not by which is newest: the operating system, the image and orchestration, or the code alone.
  • EC2's four terms — instance, instance type, AMI, security group — and its three purchasing forms are asked for by name.
  • Serverless billing is per invocation and per execution duration, and nothing is billed while the function is not running. Both halves matter.
  • Statelessness is what makes automatic scaling possible, so state has to move to storage or a database. An answer that puts state in the function contradicts the model.
  • The costs of serverless are the flip side of its conveniences: a capped execution time and cold starts. A list of benefits alone is incomplete.
  • Region against availability zone is a fault-domain distinction, and the rule that follows from it is placing replicas across zones.

Full-marks answer

  1. Name the three compute shapes and the division of labour between them, with the platform services in each.
  2. Describe EC2 as a web service for elastic compute, name its monitor and templates, and define instance, instance type, AMI and security group.
  3. Give the three purchasing forms and their trade, then auto-scaling as demand-driven provisioning turned into a service.
  4. Define serverless, give its properties — event-driven, per-invocation billing, automatic scaling, statelessness — and then its costs.
  5. Describe Compute Engine and say what distinguishes it, then explain the convergence of the three platforms through their APIs and why lock-in is only partial.
  6. Finish with how a platform is used and organised: console, API, command-line interface and SDKs; region and availability zone; the reference architecture and the design goals of the stack.

8.1.html:
In one line

Cloud data security is the problem of protecting data in each of the states it can be in — in transit, at rest, and during multi-tenancy processing — while privacy answers who may hold personal data and compliance answers the rules that follow the data through its whole life cycle.

The explanation

Data security covers four things, three of which are the states the data can be in. Data in transit is protected by a secured protocol or by encrypting the payload, which gives both confidentiality and integrity. Data at rest is generally not encrypted, because it is commingled with other users' data on shared storage — and encryption alone would defeat indexing, which is what makes an unencrypted store searchable and therefore useful. Multitenancy means processing needs the data readable, so the trust placed in the platform is not replaced by cryptography: a machine that must compute on the plaintext cannot be secured by encrypting it. Data lineage records when and where the data was, through an identifier, a timestamp and an endpoint. Two research directions aim at the combination that the first two states make hard, confidentiality and searchability together: homomorphic encryption and predicate encryption.

Data provenance extends lineage from the data to the computation. The exchange rate quoted, the location of the system and the state of the machine are all unverifiable to the customer: the workload ran on a machine the customer does not own, in a jurisdiction they may not know, at a time they cannot check. The distinction to state plainly is that integrity of data is not integrity of computation — the bytes can be perfectly untouched while the result is wrong.

Data remanence is the risk of inadvertent disclosure: data that remains where it was not intended to remain. It connects directly to storage virtualization, because if a customer does not know which physical disks hold their blocks, proving that a deleted copy is gone is harder than deleting it. Centralisation is the second exposure: quantities of data from many companies in one place make the collection an attractive target for criminals, and the physical security of the data centre and the trustworthiness of the system administrators become the customer's risk rather than the customer's control.

Privacy varies among countries, cultures and jurisdictions, shaped by public expectations and legal interpretations, which is why a concise definition is elusive. Privacy rights concern the collection, use, disclosure, storage and destruction of personal data, and come down to the accountability of organisations and the transparency of their practices. Five concerns are named as the working set: storage, retention, destruction, auditing and breaches — with data residency, where the data is required to sit, among the storage questions.

Compliance is managed over a data life cycle, and two rules govern it: personal information is managed as part of the organisation's data rather than as a separate category, and protection must consider the cloud's impact at each phase. The seven phases are generation, transformation, transfer, use, storage, archival and destruction. The cloud changes the risk at each one in a specific way: transfer crosses legal regimes, use needs the data readable and therefore exposed during processing, and destruction is a request to a provider rather than an act the customer performs.

How it runs

Follow one personal record through the life cycle in a cloud deployment. It is generated at a branch office, transformed into a record in a customer system, and transferred to a provider's storage in another country. The transfer is the phase where the legal regime changes, so residency and the terms of the contract decide whether the transfer was permitted at all.

In use, the record must be readable, which is the phase encryption cannot cover: an application computing on a value needs the value, so the protection during use rests on the platform's isolation and on access control rather than on cryptography. At rest it sits on shared storage alongside other tenants' data, which is where centralisation turns many small risks into one large target and where remanence becomes a question about physical disks nobody names.

Archival moves the cost down and the retention question up: how long may it be kept, and who decides. Destruction is the last phase and the most asymmetric one, because the customer asks the provider to delete and then has to take the answer on trust — with replication meaning there was never one copy to delete in the first place.

Exam traps

  • The three states of data are in transit, at rest and during processing under multi-tenancy, and the fourth item is lineage. Each state has its own protection and its own limit, and the limits are the marks.
  • Data at rest is generally not encrypted in the cloud, and the reason is commingling with other users' data and the fact that encryption defeats indexing. "Because it is expensive" is not the reason given.
  • Integrity of data against integrity of computation is the provenance distinction, and it is asked for in exactly those terms.
  • Data remanence is about proving a copy is gone when the physical disks are not known, and it is tied to storage virtualization and to replication.
  • Privacy's five concerns are storage, retention, destruction, auditing and breaches, with residency among the storage questions.
  • The seven life-cycle phases are generation, transformation, transfer, use, storage, archival and destruction, and the three phases that the cloud changes most are transfer, use and destruction.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the states of data and the fourth area, and for each state the protection and its limit.
  2. Name the two research directions aimed at confidentiality with searchability, and say what problem they answer.
  3. Define data provenance and make the data against computation point, with the three things a customer cannot verify.
  4. Define remanence, connect it to storage virtualization, and add centralisation and the human risk of administration.
  5. Set out privacy: why a definition is elusive, the rights involved, the accountability and transparency basis, and the five concerns with residency.
  6. Close with compliance: the two governing rules and the seven phases of the life cycle, naming how the cloud changes transfer, use and destruction.
