8.2.html:
In one line

IAM — identity and access management — is a framework of policies and technologies that ensures the right individuals get the right access to the right resources, and in the cloud it matters more than on premises because the organization's control becomes identity rather than network location.

The explanation

The components are what has to be listed. Authentication verifies identity, through something such as a username and password or multi-factor authentication. Authorization defines permissions and actions: what an authenticated party is allowed to do. User management handles accounts, groups and roles, and in the cloud permissions attach to roles rather than to individuals, which is how they stay manageable at scale. Policy enforcement applies the security policies, and audit logs record and monitor activity so that what happened can be reconstructed afterwards. One identity spanning many services is federated identity, and it appears to the user as single sign-on.

Why the cloud makes this a different problem rather than the same one in a new place is the second half of the topic, and it has five reasons. The organisation's trust boundary becomes dynamic and moves beyond its control, into the provider's domain — so the perimeter that used to define what was inside no longer does. Access must serve diverse user populations — employees, contractors and partners — which means more authentication events across more kinds of account. Higher-assurance authentication is needed, because authentication may happen outside the firewall where the organisation cannot see the attempt, and passwords have known limits. Users authenticate from mobile devices, over networks the organisation does not control. And the conclusion that ties the five together: the control becomes identity rather than network location.

How it runs

A person reaching a cloud resource, with the controls in order. They authenticate to an identity provider, which may be the organisation's own or the provider's, and receive a credential carrying what they are — the authentication step. A group or role is attached to that identity, and the policy that applies to the role says what may be done — the authorization step.

No network address is consulted at any point. The request arrives at the service as an API call with a credential attached, and what admits or refuses it is the policy attached to the identity that presented the credential, not the position of the machine making the call. That is the single sentence that distinguishes cloud access control from the firewall rules it replaces.

Now audit it. Every decision is a recorded event, so the question after an incident is answerable: which identity acted, under which policy, and when the policy last changed. Two consequences follow from the same design. Because permissions attach to roles rather than to people, a person leaving is a role change rather than a hunt through every service for their access. And because one identity can span services, a compromised credential is not confined to one of them — which is why multi-factor authentication and short-lived credentials, rather than longer passwords, are the controls the cloud asks for.

Exam traps

  • The components are authentication, authorization, user management with accounts, groups and roles, policy enforcement, and audit. Naming only authentication and authorization is half an answer.
  • Permissions attach to roles at cloud scale, which is what keeps them manageable. That detail is worth writing.
  • The five reasons IAM matters more in the cloud are the dynamic trust boundary, diverse user populations, higher-assurance authentication, mobile devices and networks outside the organisation's control, and the shift of control to identity.
  • Federated identity and single sign-on are named, and single sign-on is the appearance of one identity across services rather than a separate mechanism.
  • The last reason is the conclusion: control becomes identity rather than network location. An answer that ends on "more users" misses the point.
  • Audit logging is a component of IAM, not an afterthought, because it is what makes authorization decisions reviewable after the fact.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define IAM and give the three rights it arranges — the right individuals, the right access, the right resources.
  2. List its components: authentication with its forms, authorization, user management with accounts, groups and roles, policy enforcement, and audit.
  3. State why permissions attach to roles rather than individuals as the estate grows, and define federated identity and single sign-on.
  4. Give the five reasons IAM matters more in the cloud, one line each, starting from the trust boundary.
  5. Follow one access request through authentication, authorization and audit, showing that no network location is consulted.
  6. Close on the conclusion: the control is identity, and the practical consequences are role-based grants and the need for stronger authentication of credentials that span services.

8.3.html:
In one line

A service level agreement is the service contract with a provider: a guaranteed minimum level and a target level, with metrics and service objectives, and a remedy when the minimum is missed.

The explanation

A complete statement names the service, the metric, the minimum and the target, and the remedy. An agreement is per service — compute, storage, networking and support agreements each cover one account at once — and the remedy is usually a service credit rather than compensation for lost business. Two consequences of that shape are worth stating: meeting the minimum means there has been no breach, which is not the same as good service, and the credit is a fraction of the bill rather than a measure of the loss.

The five criteria are the substance of the agreement, and each measures something different. Availability: the percentage of time the service is guaranteed to be available. Performance: response time and throughput. Disaster recovery: the mean time to recover. Problem resolution: the process for identifying problems, with the support options and the resolution expectations. Security and privacy of data: the mechanisms for data in storage and in transmission. Availability is the criterion that rewards arithmetic, because it is a percentage of a period: 99.9% of a thirty-day month is about 43 minutes of allowed downtime, while 99.99% is about 4.3 minutes — and that difference of one nine is the difference between a rounding error and an outage someone notices.

The agreement has a life cycle of five phases, from the identification of terms to termination. Contract definition: offerings and agreements are defined from standard templates, which together form a catalogue. Publishing and discovery: the offerings are advertised and customers search the catalogue. Negotiation: the terms are agreed and signed off. Operationalization: monitoring, accounting and enforcement, with policies expressible in a common information model. De-commissioning: the termination of all activities under the agreement.

Distinct from the contract's life is the life of the hosted application, which has its own five phases. Feasibility: a study of technical, infrastructure and financial feasibility. On-boarding: the application moves to the platform and is profiled so that policies for its service level objectives can be created. Pre-production: a simulated production environment in which the customer validates the findings. Production: the application is live, and sustained breaches send it back to on-boarding rather than simply incurring a penalty. Termination: data returns to the customer, with only essential information kept.

How it runs

A month of service against one agreement. The provider commits to an availability percentage and publishes it; the customer's monitoring measures what actually happened, and the two figures are compared at the end of the period. If the service was above the minimum, there is no breach — even if performance was poor enough to be noticed, because each criterion is measured separately.

If availability fell below the minimum, the operationalization machinery takes over: the breach is recorded against the agreement, the credit is calculated from the committed terms, and nothing about the customer's actual losses enters the arithmetic. Sustained breaches matter differently for a hosted application, because they send it back to on-boarding — the application is profiled again and its objectives are re-derived from the standing environment rather than patched with a penalty.

At the end of the relationship the de-commissioning phase terminates every activity under the agreement, and the application's own termination phase returns the data to the customer with only what is essential kept. The two life cycles meet at exactly one point — the moment the service stops — which is why they are taught as two lists rather than one.

Exam traps

  • A complete agreement names the service, the metric, the minimum, the target and the remedy. Leaving out the remedy turns a contract into a description.
  • The remedy is a service credit, not compensation for lost business, and meeting the minimum is not good service. Both are short statements that earn marks.
  • An agreement is per service, so a single account is covered by several of them at once.
  • The five criteria are availability, performance, disaster recovery, problem resolution, and security and privacy of data.
  • The availability arithmetic is examinable: 99.9% of a thirty-day month is about 43 minutes and 99.99% is about 4.3 minutes. Quote the period as well as the percentage.
  • The contract's five phases and the hosted application's five phases are two different lists: contract definition, publishing and discovery, negotiation, operationalization, de-commissioning against feasibility, on-boarding, pre-production, production, termination. Swapping a phase between them is the standard error.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define an agreement and the elements a complete statement contains.
  2. State that agreements are per service, that the remedy is usually a service credit, and that meeting the minimum is not good service.
  3. Give the five criteria with what each one measures.
  4. Work the availability arithmetic for a thirty-day month at two levels, and say what the difference means.
  5. Give the five phases of the contract's life cycle in order.
  6. Give the five phases of the hosted application's life, note that a sustained breach returns it to on-boarding, and say what termination returns to the customer.

8.4.html:
In one line

Cloud risk is managed by matching the eight common vulnerabilities against the eight mitigation control areas, under the shared responsibility model that divides security between the provider's platform and the customer's configuration, identities, data and code.

The explanation

The eight vulnerabilities come first, and each is a specific failure rather than a general worry. Data breaches: unauthorised access through misconfigured storage, weak access controls or poor encryption. Insecure APIs: weak authentication or missing input validation, and since the API surface is the attack surface, a weak interface is the whole way in. Misconfigurations: overly permissive buckets, open security groups and weak firewall rules. Account hijacking: compromised credentials abused to exfiltrate data or to spend the victim's resources. Denial of service: elastic capacity means an attack can be billed to the victim, so the attack costs money even when it does not succeed. Then insider threats, shared technology risks and legal risks complete the eight.

The eight control areas answer them with practices. Data security: encrypt in transit and at rest, and manage keys with a key management service or a hardware security module. Identity and access management: least privilege, multi-factor authentication, short-lived credentials and deny-by-default. Secure APIs: standard authorisation with tokens, input validation, rate limiting and a web application firewall. Configuration management: posture management, vulnerability scanning and policy as code. Threat detection & monitoring: centralised logging and a security information and event management system, with anomaly detection. Then denial-of-service resilience, vendor diligence and training make up the eight.

The shared responsibility model is the division of duty, and it explains why the vulnerability list looks the way it does. The provider secures the cloud: the physical facility, the hardware, the hypervisor and the managed services underneath. The customer secures in the cloud: their configuration, their identities, their data and their code. That is why misconfiguration and insecure APIs are the customer's fault even though the platform is the provider's — the provider cannot see, and should not decide, how a customer's bucket is shared. The provider can certify the platform; knowing which side of the line each control sits on is the customer's job.

A long security question can be structured as a chain of five links. The risks: the eight vulnerabilities and the exposures of the four data states. The obligations: privacy and personal information, retention, destruction, compliance and residency. The controls: the eight control areas, with identity management and encryption as the data controls. The assurance: the service level agreement, its breach and penalty machinery, and the auditor who verifies it. The division of duty: shared responsibility and de-perimeterisation. Two of those links carry the most weight in an answer, and they are shared responsibility and shared technology.

Two challenges are worked through in full. Multi-tenancy and shared technology: tenants share hardware and a hypervisor, so a hypervisor flaw can enable cross-tenant attacks, and centralised data makes the collection an attractive target. The mitigations are patching and isolation, least privilege, monitoring and provider certification. Data confidentiality and the limits of control: data at rest is generally not encrypted, governments may search data according to residency rules, and replication makes proof of destruction hard. The mitigations are encryption with managed keys, tokenisation, residency-aware regions, contractual retention and deletion terms, and audit.

How it runs

Take a misconfigured object store and follow it as both vulnerability and control. A bucket is created for a workload and left readable by anyone who knows its name. This is the misconfiguration vulnerability, and it is squarely on the customer's side of the shared responsibility line: the provider supplied a bucket and a policy language, and the customer chose the policy.

The control that would have caught it is configuration management — posture management that continuously compares the deployed configuration against the intended one, finds the bucket that permits public reads, and reports it before an attacker does. The vulnerability is a mistake and the control is a comparison, which is why policy as code is part of the answer: a rule that is written down can be checked continuously, while an intention cannot.

Now trace the same event through the assurance link. The breach or near-miss is visible in centralised logs; the auditor's role is to verify conformance to standards rather than to trust the report; and the service level agreement decides whether the customer has any remedy at all when the provider's part of the line was crossed. Risk management here is not one control but the chain: what can go wrong, what must be protected, what prevents it, who proves it, and which side of the line it sits on.

Exam traps

  • The eight vulnerabilities are asked for as a named set: data breaches, insecure APIs, misconfigurations, account hijacking, denial of service, insider threats, shared technology risks and legal risks.
  • The elastic capacity point is the reason a denial-of-service attack is a billing risk as well as an availability risk, and it is specific to the cloud.
  • The eight control areas pair with the vulnerabilities, so the answer should say which control answers which risk rather than listing both.
  • Least privilege, multi-factor authentication, short-lived credentials and deny-by-default belong to identity and access management.
  • The shared responsibility sentence must be split correctly: the provider secures the cloud, the customer secures in the cloud. Misconfiguration and insecure APIs being the customer's fault follows from that split.
  • Multi-tenancy and data confidentiality are the two worked challenges, each with its mechanisms and its mitigations, and centralisation makes the collection a target — a different point from any single breach.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the eight vulnerabilities with a clause each, marking misconfiguration and insecure APIs as the customer's side.
  2. Give the eight control areas, pairing each with the risk it answers.
  3. State the shared responsibility model: what the provider secures and what the customer secures, and the consequence for misconfiguration.
  4. Set out the five-link structure of a long security answer: risks, obligations, controls, assurance and division of duty.
  5. Work the multi-tenancy and shared technology challenge with its mechanisms and mitigations.
  6. Work the data confidentiality and limits-of-control challenge with its mechanisms and mitigations, ending on the controls that remain once the perimeter is gone.

9.1.html:
In one line

Cloud computing consolidated resources into large data centres, and edge and fog computing are the counter-movement: compute is placed where latency and bandwidth allow it, and only what must be central stays central.

The explanation

The reason is physics rather than fashion. Sending all device data to a distant data centre costs latency, bandwidth and sometimes privacy or legal compliance, and it fails entirely when the device is offline. No amount of capacity in the data centre answers a round trip to another continent or a link that is not there.

The progression happened in three steps: content at the edge, which is the content-delivery network; then edge servers assisting; then fog computing, where end-user devices form part of the system rather than merely consuming it. The three tiers are told apart by where the compute sits relative to the data source, not by what technology they use. Edge is the devices themselves: milliseconds of latency, tiny compute, real-time control and the ability to work offline. Fog is nodes near the edge — gateways, cell towers, on-premise servers — one local network hop away, shared by many devices. Cloud is the data centre: the elastic pool with unlimited capacity and global reach, which is where training, archives and heavy analytics belong.

What the move buys is a short list and what it costs is another. It buys latency, because a control loop cannot wait for a round trip to another continent. It buys bandwidth and cost, because filtering at the edge is the difference between sending events and sending video. It buys privacy and compliance, because processing where the data was produced keeps regulated data inside a jurisdiction. And it buys availability, because a device that keeps working without connectivity keeps working. It costs in the number of nodes to manage, weaker physical security than a data centre has, updates that have to reach a fleet rather than a rack, and clock synchronisation between thousands of devices — which is the same problem the synchronisation unit began with, now with far more clocks.

How it runs

A camera with a detection model, run both ways. In the centralised design every frame goes to the data centre for inference. The frame is large, the round trip is tens of milliseconds at best, and a link that drops takes the whole function with it. The bandwidth bill grows with the number of cameras and with the frame rate rather than with the number of interesting events.

Move the inference to the device and the same function is local: the frame is analysed where it was captured, in milliseconds, with no network in the path, and the link carries an alert instead of a stream. The cost moves with it — every camera now runs a model that has to be updated, monitored and secured, and a camera in a street cabinet is not a data centre: its physical security is whatever the cabinet provides.

Now put only what must be central in the centre. Aggregating the alerts across sites, retraining the model, and keeping the archive all belong where capacity is elastic and cheap, because none of them is latency-sensitive. The division of labour follows from the latency requirement rather than from preference, which is the point of the topic: the tiers differ by where the compute sits relative to the data source, and the reason to move it is measured in milliseconds and in bytes not sent.

Exam traps

  • The three tiers are edge, fog and cloud, and they differ by where the compute sits relative to the data source — not by which technology each uses.
  • Fog is the middle tier and the one most often confused with edge: nodes near the devices, one local network hop away, shared by many devices.
  • The four benefits are latency, bandwidth and cost, privacy and compliance, and availability, and each needs its reason.
  • The costs are equally examinable: many more nodes to manage, weaker physical security, fleet-wide updates, and clock synchronisation across thousands of devices.
  • The three-step progression — content at the edge, then edge servers assisting, then fog — makes the counter-movement an evolution rather than a single invention.
  • Offline operation is a benefit in its own right and not a variety of latency. A device that works without connectivity is a different claim from one that answers quickly.

Full-marks answer

  1. Give the reason for the counter-movement: latency, bandwidth, privacy and compliance, and offline operation.
  2. Set out the three-step progression from content at the edge to fog computing.
  3. Describe the three tiers by where the compute sits relative to the data source, with the latency and the capacity of each.
  4. Give the four benefits with the argument for each, using the control loop and the video-stream picture as the concrete cases.
  5. Give the costs that the same distribution creates.
  6. Close on the placement rule: only what must be central is central, and the criterion is the latency requirement rather than the technology.

9.2.html:
In one line

Serverless computing is a model in which the provider runs the code and the customer provisions no servers, with function as a service — FaaS — for event-driven execution billed per invocation, and back-end as a service — BaaS — for the managed pieces a function calls instead of running its own.

The explanation

Two halves make up the model. FaaS is event-driven execution billed per invocation, on platforms such as AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google Cloud Functions. BaaS is the managed databases, queues, authentication and storage that a function calls rather than running its own — which is what makes the no-server claim hold, since a function that starts its own database is running a server somewhere after all.

The properties are a set of five, and each has consequences. Event-driven: something happens and the code runs, rather than the code waiting. No server management: there is no machine to patch, size or keep running. Automatic scaling: the platform runs as many copies as the traffic needs, which is elasticity at the granularity of a single request. Pay per use: the bill counts invocations and execution duration, so idle time is free. Stateless functions: nothing survives between invocations, so state belongs in storage or a database. The trade is stated in one line: control is given up for convenience, and steady high load is cheaper on a reserved machine.

Where serverless fits is a list, and where it does not fit is the sharper half of the answer. It fits glue between services, such as a file arriving in storage and triggering a resize or an index update; scheduled and administrative jobs such as nightly reports, cleanup and backups, which are minutes of work a day; sporadic traffic, such as an internal tool, a webhook endpoint or an API used in bursts; and an event-driven application, where each step of a workflow consumes the previous step's event. It is wrong for long-running processes, for stateful services, for latency-critical workloads where a cold start is unacceptable, and for steady high load.

How it runs

Follow one image upload. A client puts an object into storage. The storage service emits an event, and the event invokes a function — nothing was running before that moment, and there was no machine waiting for the upload. The function reads the object, produces a resized copy, writes it back, and returns. Billing counted one invocation and the milliseconds it took.

Now the same application under a burst of uploads. Each event invokes an instance of the function, and the platform runs as many of them at once as the arrivals need, so the throughput rises without anyone choosing a number of machines. When the burst ends, the instances stop existing and the billing stops with them — which is what makes the cost model fit work that arrives in peaks.

Then the two costs show. If a request arrives after an idle period, the platform has to prepare an environment for the function, and the first request waits for that preparation — the cold start — which is why a latency-critical path is the wrong place for one. And if the traffic is steady and high, the per-invocation arithmetic eventually exceeds the price of a machine that is simply left running, which is why the same workload moves back to containers or a reserved instance as its load becomes predictable.

Exam traps

  • The two halves of the model are function as a service and back-end as a service, and both are needed for the no-server claim to be true.
  • The five properties are event-driven execution, no server management, automatic scaling, pay per use, and stateless functions.
  • Statelessness is not a limitation to complain about; it is the property that makes per-request scaling and cheap billing possible, and the answer should say so.
  • The workloads it suits are glue, scheduled jobs, sporadic traffic and event-driven workflows. The workloads it does not suit are long-running processes, stateful services, latency-critical paths and steady high load.
  • Billing is per invocation and per execution duration. Quoting only one of the two understates the model.
  • Cold start is the named cost of the latency-critical case, and the reserved machine is the named alternative for steady load. Both are asked for by name.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define serverless and give the two halves of the model with their platforms and their role.
  2. Give the five properties, explaining what each one implies for the customer.
  3. State the trade: control given up for convenience, and steady high load cheaper on a reserved machine.
  4. List the four workloads serverless fits, with the example of each.
  5. List the four workloads it does not fit, with the reason of each, naming the cold start as the latency reason.
  6. Close by following one event through the model — trigger, invocation, execution, billing — and showing where the idle period costs nothing.

9.3.html:
In one line

Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a container image, and Kubernetes schedules, heals and scales those containers across a cluster — the packaging and the orchestration of the same idea.

The explanation

A container is a unit of software that is lightweight but still bundles the code, its dependencies and the configuration into a single image. Unlike a virtual machine it shares the host system kernel, and is therefore more resource-efficient. Four terms carry the toolchain: an image is the packaged unit, frozen and immutable once built; a Dockerfile is the recipe that builds it, which is what makes the environment reproducible; a registry is where images are stored and fetched, which is what turns a build into a deployment; and the container engine is what runs the container, on bare metal, on hypervisors or in cloud infrastructure.

Why an orchestrator is needed is the argument of the topic. A production system is many containers across many machines, and Docker does not solve four problems: placement, which container runs on which node; restarts and self-healing, replacing what crashes; scaling, adding copies when load rises; and networking and discovery, because callers need a stable name for a set of containers that is constantly changing. Kubernetes solves them by declaring the desired state and continuously working to match it — the cluster is told what should be true, and it keeps making it true. Three pieces of its vocabulary matter: a pod is the smallest deployable unit, a service is a stable name in front of a changing set of pods, and managed Kubernetes is the provider running the control plane.

The security caveat is the price of the sharing that makes containers efficient. Containers are not free isolation: the cons include less security from sharing the operating system. A virtual machine's boundary is enforced by the hypervisor, while a container's is enforced by the kernel it shares with its neighbours, so any kernel flaw crosses it — the Meltdown vulnerability was one such flaw. And the first process in a container normally runs as root, so an escape yields root on the host rather than an unprivileged account. The hardening list follows directly: run as a non-root user, drop unneeded capabilities, mount file systems read-only, apply a seccomp or AppArmor profile, and patch the host kernel.

How it runs

From source to running workload. A Dockerfile is written, and building it produces an image — a frozen, reproducible artifact that contains the code and its dependencies. The image is pushed to a registry, so what a deployment fetches is exactly what was built and tested, which is the part of the story that removes the environment as a source of surprises.

The cluster is then given a declared state: so many copies of this image, reachable under this name, with these resources. The orchestrator compares that declaration with what exists and acts on the difference — starting pods on nodes with room, replacing ones that have died, and adding copies when the load rises. Nobody issues a command for each of those events; the difference between declared and actual is what drives the work.

Now approach it as an attacker or as a hardened operator. The pod runs on a shared kernel, so the boundary between it and its neighbour is the kernel's own isolation rather than a hypervisor's; a flaw in that isolation reaches the host, and because the first process is usually root, what it reaches is privileged. Hardening is therefore a list of deliberate reductions — non-root user, dropped capabilities, read-only mounts, a seccomp or AppArmor profile — and keeping the list current means patching the host kernel, because the boundary that protects every container on that host is the one they all share.

Exam traps

  • The four vocabulary terms are image, Dockerfile, registry and container engine, and each is defined by its role rather than by its technology.
  • The orchestrator's four problems are placement, restarts and self-healing, scaling, and networking with discovery. Docker solves packaging and not these.
  • Declarative desired state is Kubernetes's central idea: the cluster is told what should be true and works continuously to make it true.
  • A pod is the smallest deployable unit and a service is a stable name in front of changing pods. Swapping the two definitions is the standard error.
  • The container security boundary is the shared kernel, not a hypervisor, and Meltdown is the named example of a flaw that crosses it.
  • Running as root is what makes an escape severe, and the hardening list — non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only mounts, seccomp or AppArmor, patched host kernel — is the answer to it.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define the container and the image, and give the four toolchain terms with their roles.
  2. State why an orchestrator is needed, by listing the four problems Docker does not solve.
  3. Explain Kubernetes's declarative model and define pod, service and managed Kubernetes.
  4. Give the security caveat: the shared kernel as the boundary, the kernel flaw that crosses it, and root as the severity multiplier.
  5. List the hardening measures in order, from the user the process runs as to patching the host kernel.
  6. Close by following an image from a Dockerfile through a registry to a running pod, and showing where the declared state does the work.

In one line

Cloud-native means treating the cloud's properties as given rather than as a place to host something built for a server, and its central structure is a microservice architecture — small independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over a network interface.

The explanation

The defining move is an assumption: the application assumes the platform is elastic, programmable, failure-prone and disposable, so it is built from small independently deployable services. Lift-and-shift is the opposite, and it inherits the cloud's costs without its benefits — the same application, moved, still expects a machine that stays up and still cannot use elasticity, self-healing or pay-per-use. Cloud-native changes the design so that those properties become usable.

The characteristics are a named set: microservices, containers, orchestration, declarative configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous delivery, observability and horizontal scaling. Read as a list rather than a story, they describe an application whose shape was chosen for a platform that fails in pieces.

The microservice architecture itself structures an application as small independently deployable services. Against a monolith the differences are four: scaling is per service rather than the whole application; deployment is independent, so one service can be released without the others; each service can use its own technology; and a fault is contained rather than taking the application with it. The cost is stated just as plainly. Each service owns its data, so consistency across services replaces the distributed transactions that a single database used to provide, and partial failure becomes normal rather than exceptional. The real cost is distributed systems: splitting an application converts local calls into remote calls, which brings latency, marshalling and call semantics with it — the same three concerns the communication unit began with.

How the tools support the architecture is an argument in four steps rather than a stack. Microservices create the need for packaging, because each service must arrive with its dependencies intact. Packaging creates the need for orchestration, because an image is static and something must place it and keep the copies alive. Many moving services create the need for delivery and observability, because failures are partial and therefore not visible on any one machine. And each step costs: remote calls between services, a weaker boundary than a hypervisor's, and an orchestration layer that is itself a distributed system with its own failures.

Two halves make the topic answerable in one pass. What cloud-native architecture is: the definition, the eight characteristics, and the contrast with lift-and-shift. How each tool supports it: microservices provide the structure, containers provide the packaging, and orchestration provides the operation that keeps the declared replica count alive and replaces what fails.

How it runs

Take one feature inside a monolith and move it out. In the monolith the feature runs in the same process as everything else: its call into another part of the system is a function call, and a fault anywhere in the process is a fault in the whole application. Scaling means running the whole application again, because there is nothing smaller to scale.

As a service it is packaged as an image, deployed independently, given its own data store, and reached over the network. It now scales on its own — copies are added when its load rises, and nothing else is duplicated to get them. A fault in it is contained: the other services keep answering, and the failure appears as one kind of error on one call path instead of as an outage.

And the bill for those gains arrives immediately. The call that used to be a function call is now a remote call, with latency, marshalling and call semantics attached to it. The transaction that used to span one database now spans several, so consistency becomes an application problem. Partial failure is now normal, which is why delivery and observability are on the characteristics list rather than being operational extras: nothing on any single machine shows whether the system as a whole is healthy, so the design has to make that visible.

Exam traps

  • The definition turns on an assumption — that the platform is elastic, programmable, failure-prone and disposable — and lift-and-shift's failure to make that assumption is the contrast to give.
  • The eight characteristics are a named set: microservices, containers, orchestration, declarative configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous delivery, observability and horizontal scaling.
  • Microservices against a monolith has four differences — per-service scaling, independent deployment, technology choice per service, and fault containment — and the cost on the other side.
  • The cost of microservices is distributed systems: local calls become remote calls, data ownership spreads, and partial failure becomes normal. An answer with only the benefits is incomplete.
  • Each service owning its data is what replaces the single database's transactions with an application-level consistency problem.
  • The four-step support argument is need then tool: packaging, orchestration, delivery and observability. Each step has its own cost.

Full-marks answer

  1. Define cloud-native by the assumptions it makes about the platform, and contrast it with lift-and-shift.
  2. Give the eight characteristics.
  3. Define a microservice architecture through the four differences from a monolith.
  4. Give the costs: per-service data ownership replacing transactions, contained faults at the price of partial failure, and remote calls in place of local ones.
  5. Give the four-step argument for how the tools support the architecture, with the cost at each step.
  6. Close with the two halves of the topic — what the architecture is, and how each tool supports it — and with the trends seen as a whole: moving computation, and changing how an application is built.
